World.title: Conflict shift
World.content:
Superintendent Mark Harris, commanding officer for the St Andrew Central Police Division, speaks about the division’s changing crime landscape during an episode of the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s Force4Good podcast. x

THE St Andrew Central Police Division, which is the commercial heartbeat of the Corporate Area, where thousands of Jamaicans live and work daily, is confronting a changing crime landscape, with police saying interpersonal and domestic conflicts have become a greater concern than organised gang violence.

Commanding officer for the St Andrew Central Police Division Superintendent Mark Harris said the division has largely brought organised gang activity under control, but is now grappling with murders arising from personal disputes, many of which occur without warning and in communities not traditionally associated with violent crime. He said this shift has presented a more complex policing challenge because, unlike gang conflicts, interpersonal disputes are far less predictable.

Speaking on the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s (JCF) Force4Good podcast, Harris said the division recorded the largest reduction in murders across the Jamaica Constabulary Force last year and even went an entire month without a murder this February. However, he noted that while gang-related killings have declined significantly, police are increasingly being challenged by crimes rooted in personal and domestic disputes.

“Last year, I had gang issues, [but] this year, we don’t have a gang issue, we have criminals committing crimes, but it’s not associated with gangs, like 2024 and part of 2025, and believe it or not, gang conflict is easier to police than the interpersonal and the domestic issues,” he noted.

The St Andrew Central Police Division encompasses some of Jamaica’s busiest commercial, educational and transport hubs, including Half-Way-Tree, New Kingston, Cross Roads and Papine. It is also responsible for policing major national events, entertainment activities and sporting fixtures that are often held at the National Stadium, making it one of the JCF’s most demanding divisions.

The division also includes communities such as August Town and Nannyville, both of which have experienced persistent gang activity and periodic security operations over the years. August Town was placed under a Zone of Special Operations in 2020 following years of deadly gang violence, while Nannyville has repeatedly featured in anti-gang and anti-gun operations as police sought to dismantle organised criminal networks operating across Kingston and St Andrew.

Despite that history, Harris said the division’s greatest challenge is no longer organised gangs but the rise in deadly interpersonal conflicts.

“We know where the gangs are and where they operate and who they’re in conflict with, and we put police right there…but for the interpersonal things, even in Jack’s Hill we have murders [and] that is not normally a place where we have murders… and these are interpersonal, rather than gang conflict,” he explained.

He said the division is relying not only on intelligence-led operations but also stronger community partnerships to prevent personal disputes from escalating into violence.

“We go out there and do the hard policing, we still have our community engagement. We had to do those meetings at the Transport Centre to speak to students and parents and stakeholders,” Harris noted.

Meanwhile, Area Four Commander Assistant Commissioner of Police Michael Phipps said St Andrew Central remains critical to crime management across Kingston and St Andrew because of its concentration of commercial activity, major institutions and daily commuter traffic.

He noted that the division has also experienced a significant number of fatal attacks involving weapons other than firearms, reflecting the growing challenge posed by interpersonal violence.

“I can tell you here and now that St Andrew Central has had a very high number of murders resulting from the use of knives and other blunt-force trauma injuries that have resulted in death. So we see St Andrew Central as one of the most important divisions if we are to maintain control of crime across Area Four,” Phipps said.

World.title: Upper St Andrew residents ready to protest
World.content:
The residents of Kingston 8 claim that a lot of the problems they face stem from an increase in large real estate projects in the area, as when projects are being executed, roads are dug up and not repaired properly. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

SOME residents of upper St Andrew have threatened to take up placards to protest poor road infrastructure and unrestricted real estate developments, as they say they are tired of their cries falling on deaf ears.

The Jamaica Observer was taken on a tour of Waterworks Road and adjoining thoroughfares in Kingston 8, starting from the Manor Park area, where various roadways that were recently patched have already started disintegrating.

The residents claim that a lot of the problems they face stem from an increase in large real estate projects in the area, as when projects are being executed, roads are dug up and not repaired properly. They also suspect that unregulated construction is a main factor in roads being damaged frequently even after being fixed.

“We are planning a protest, if nothing happens,” one resident threatened.

That resident, who withheld his name, pointed to a spot where water was spouting through a break in the asphalt on Waterworks Road. “They don’t use shingles or anything like that when they are fixing the roads, so the road is being eaten out from underneath,” he said.

As it relates to apartment projects being undertaken in the area, the resident said the road infrastructure can’t support the developments.

Pointing to premises on Waterworks Road where heavy-duty trucks used in construction were parked, the resident said the community has no idea what the plans for the location are, and is opposed to any more major construction projects at this time. Attempts have been made by members of the community to acquire information from the authorities about the developers’ plans, but they have hit a roadblock, having been told by authorities that they can get a copy of the documents in 60 days. However, this time frame poses a problem for the residents who said they are aware that under the law, they have a limited period in which to file an objection to any proposed construction projects.

In a letter recently penned by residents, which the

Observer saw, the residents said, “For nearly two years, residents of Broadway Close, Broadway Road, Sharrow Drive, and Waterworks Road in Kingston 8 have endured a slow-motion disaster. A developer dug up their roads to lay sewer pipes, left the reinstatement in a dangerously substandard condition, and vanished — while the authorities responsible for enforcing the law have failed to act. The result is that a car recently hit a sinkhole in a patched section and got stuck. Inferior patching work has crumbled under the weight of daily traffic. And residents are left asking a question that echoes across Jamaica: why are the laws on the books not being enforced?”

It continued: “The Parochial Roads Act gives the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC) clear and unequivocal authority over parochial roads like Broadway Road and Waterworks Road. It requires any developer digging up a public road to obtain a road-opening permit and provide a refundable security deposit — money held by the KSAMC to ensure that if the developer fails to properly restore the road, the corporation can do the job using those funds,” the letter stated.

“…On Broadway Road and Waterworks Road, the developer dug up the roads, laid pipes, and left behind inferior patching that has deteriorated into sinkholes and dangerous driving conditions. The KSAMC’s preliminary finding, confirmed by Member of Parliament for the area Delano Seiveright, is clear.

“But where is the accountability? If [a security deposit] was obtained [from the developer], why hasn’t it been used to fix the roads? If none was obtained, why was the developer allowed to dig up public roads without providing the required guarantee?“

Seiveright, meanwhile, said he shared the frustration of residents, stating that their concerns are legitimate and that he has been lobbying on their behalf for a remedy.

“It is important to note that the Waterworks issue pre-dates my election as Member of Parliament [for St Andrew North Central],“ he pointed out. ”Since taking office, I have met repeatedly with officials at the highest levels of the Ministry of Water, the National Water Commission (NWC), KSAMC, and the National Environment and Planning Agency, carried out several site visits and technical walk-throughs, and spoken directly with many affected residents. I also escalated the matter to Minister [of Water] Matthew Samuda.“

He said the situation in Waterworks centres on corrective works following a private developer’s sewer project in the area. He added that while the developer is at the heart of this debacle, he is pleased that KSAMC and the NWC are now working assiduously to deliver a proper resolution.

Seiveright said his advocacy has also helped to prompt a broader review of how these projects are supervised, with stronger oversight and policy improvements now being actively pursued.

“I am aware of similar issues in other communities. More broadly, residents have raised concerns about overdevelopment, infrastructure capacity and protecting community character. I share those concerns. Development must be responsible, properly planned and supported by adequate infrastructure. I have consistently conveyed residents’ views to the relevant authorities and have encouraged stronger community organisation,“ he explained.

“The Orange Grove/Bridgemount Citizens’ Association is an excellent example of the kind of united, constructive leadership that helps communities achieve results. I will continue to press vigorously for better communication with residents, stronger enforcement where necessary, and practical solutions that protect both our communities and their quality of life,” he said.

World.title: Saint International’s Fashion Face of the Caribbean set for August 29
World.content:
From left: Deiwight Peters, founder, CEO of Saint International; model Kai Newman; Member of Parliament for St Andrew Eastern and Minister of Finance Fayval Williams, and Saint International model Carolyn Sangster.Samuel Edie

For 26 years Saint International has been the leading model agency across the region, unearthing new talent each year who have gone on to achieve success on the international fashion scene.

A new set of model hopefuls are poised for international success after more than 30 were selected on Sunday, July 26 during a Saint International Community Model Search, which took place at Jamaica College.

This was the fifth model search to have taken place this year and, according to Saint International boss Deiwight Peters, this one was the biggest thus far.

“This model search is the last in the series, and we’ve had five so far. I do believe this was the biggest one; not only in terms of the size of the turnout, but certainly the faces that turned out, they were remarkable. I do feel strongly that on August 29, when we have the finals of the Fashion Face of the Caribbean competition (for both male and female), several of these new discoveries will go on to bigger things,” Peters told the Jamaica Observer shortly after the model search ended.

“We have several top agencies who will be coming in for the event, who are representing the major fashion markets in New York, London, Milan, Paris, Germany, and even Spain and they are just excited to be coming to Jamaica,” shared Peters.

Member of Parliament for St Andrew Eastern and Minister of Finance and the Public Service Fayval Williams, who was in attendance at the model search, heaped praises on Peters.

“Well, I was impressed to see the young people come out for the model search because I know there is still talent all over Jamaica. Deiwight is a very reputable person, his agency has an impressive track record, and I have no doubt that several of these model hopefuls here today will become stars of tomorrow under Deiwight’s guidance,” Williams told the Observer.

Peters shared that the minister’s presence validated the work that the agency has been doing over the years.

“I think that her turning up validated what we do and the purpose of the model search. She knows the success stories of Saint International. A big thank you to the Jamaica College family for hosting us, Mr Wayne Robinson, the principal, and the team,” he said.

Kai Newman, one of Saint International’s successful models, was in attendance at the model search to encourage the newbies.

“I just flew back to Jamaica so I said why not come here and meet some of the future stars and give them some advice, a little inspiration, and motivation. I just want them to believe in Deiwight, believe in Saint International, and to just be their authentic self,” Newman, who was discovered by Peters the age of 14 while walking on the street.

Newman has walked for designers including Burberry, Tommy Hilfiger, Chanel, Gucci, Calvin Klein, Prada, Bottega, among others.

Speaking on the Fashion Face of the Caribbean competition in August, Peters shared that more than 150 models from Jamaica, Canada, United States, Europe, several Caribbean countries including Guyana, will participate.

“We have roughly 150 models who will be participating in the Fashion Face of the Caribbean and they are coming from all over the world. It’s going to be awesome,” he said.

World.title: ‘Thrilled’ 76ers confirm James signing, eye NBA title run
World.content:
Lebron James Photo: AFP

NEW YORK, United States (AFP) — LeBron James has signed a contract to play for the Philadelphia 76ers, the team announced Monday, with managing owner Josh Harris “thrilled” about chances for their first NBA title since 1983.

James announced on Friday he would play for the Sixers on a two-year deal worth US$8 million, ending a weeks-long mystery over the 41-year-old superstar’s future, but the 76ers had no comment throughout the weekend.

“I am thrilled to welcome LeBron James to the Philadelphia 76ers,” ownership managing partner Harris said in a statement. “One of the greatest players in NBA history and one of the best athletes ever, his accomplishments are iconic.”

James, the NBA’s all-time scoring leader set to begin his record 24th campaign in October, is a four-time NBA champion and four-time NBA Most Valuable Player.

After winning two titles with Miami, another with hometown club Cleveland and his most recent with the Los Angeles Lakers in 2020, James could become the first NBA player to win crowns with four different teams.

James, a three-time Olympic champion and 22-time NBA All-Star, joins a Sixers roster filled with NBA stars in hopes of bringing Philadelphia an NBA title for the first time since Julius Erving led the club to the crown 43 years ago.

“I cannot wait to see LeBron alongside Jaylen Brown, VJ Edgecombe, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey, and our talented roster as we work to deliver a championship for Philly,” Harris said.

“To LeBron and his family: we are grateful you chose the 76ers, and look forward to this next chapter of your legendary career. Welcome to the 76ers!”

James has career averages of 26.8 points, 7.5 rebounds, 7.4 assists and 1.5 steals over 1,622 games.

Philadelphia 76ers president of basketball operations Mike Gansey, an Ohio high school rival of James on the court, expects the legend will boost the club and the community.

“There’s no doubt LeBron is one of the greatest players to ever play the game of basketball and there are no words to measure the impact he’ll have on this organisation,” Gansey said.

“I’ve had the pleasure of knowing LeBron since high school and have seen the high-level impact he has produced at every stop of his basketball journey. He is a consummate professional, the ultimate competitor, and a tireless worker.

“But he’s also an incredible person with natural leadership traits, a family man, and someone who possesses unwavering commitment to community and those around him. We couldn’t be happier that he’s officially here.”

The 76ers posted a photo on social media of a James jersey, keeping his tradition number 23 with his new club, hanging in a locker with a crown on a shelf inside it, a nod toward “King James” being with the Sixers.

James has taken teams into the NBA play-offs 19 times, matching a league record, with post-season averages of 28.2 points, 8.9 rebounds, 7.2 assists, 1.7 steals and 1.0 blocked shots over 302 games.

In June, James announced he was leaving the Lakers and numerous clubs were seen as contenders to become his new home, including Miami, Cleveland, Golden State and Minnesota as well as the 76ers.

Philadelphia swung a deal with Boston three weeks ago for Brown, sending Paul George to the Celtics, and together with centre Embiid and top guards Maxey and Edgecombe they provided a line-up too good for James to pass up in his quest for a fifth NBA title.

“I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energise a new fan base and start this incredible journey one last time,” James posted on X Friday.

World.title: DOUBLE JOY!
World.content:
DEMARIO Prince says a talk with his coach after the first round got his mind back where it was supposed to be, leading him to win the gold medal in the 110m hurdles on Monday’s first day of track and field at the Commonwealth Games at Scotstoun Stadium in Glasgow, Scotland.

Jamaica won two gold medals on the day as, minutes before Prince’s run, Romaine Beckford won the men’s high jump. Beckford’s leap to clear 2.25m brought Jamaica’s second gold in the event at the games and first in 68 years.

Prince, the fourth-straight Jamaican and fifth in the last six editions to win the 110m gold medal, ran 13.17 seconds (0.4m/s) to claim his first major global medal.

Prince, who was fourth in the 60m hurdles at the World Athletics Indoor Championships in March, was delighted with the win. “This means a lot. You know, that was the aim coming into the Commonwealth Games. You know, just to get the gold medal, do it for myself, my family, and the fans. So yeah, I’m very, very pleased, very happy with the win,” Prince told the Jamaica Observer.

The sprint hurdler said he believes this is the start of good things to come.

“I feel like I can still give more and still wrap up more gold medals,” he said, noting that he had not been happy with his first round race in which he placed second.

“I was more confident going into the final, I just had to go back in the mindset to know that I can go out there and execute as I was not pleased with the prelims. I spoke to coach Ben (Dalton) and he told me not to worry about anything, he told me that I can do this. It is a regular thing for me to go out and execute and go get the medal for Jamaica,” Prince said.

England’s Samuel Bennett ran a personal best 13.30 for the silver medal and Milan Trajkvoc clocked a season’s best 12.32 to deliver Cyprus’ first medal in the event. Jamaica’s Jerome Campbell was sixth in 13.86.

Beckford, who was eighth in 2022 and failed to clear the first height at last year’s World Athletics Championships, became the first Jamaican man to win the event since 1958 when Ernle Haisley set a then Commonwealth Games record 2.06m to capture gold.

India’s Sarvesh Anil Kushare, who also cleared 2.25m, took the silver medal. England’s NCAA champion Kimani Jack was third with 2.20m.

Two-time World Indoor bronze medallist Raymond Richards just missed a medal, placing fourth also with 2.20m.

Jamaica will hope to add more medals today with athletes qualified for several finals, including in the men’s and women’s 100m.

Women’s high jump defending champion Lamara Distin, former men’s 400m world champion Antonio Watson and 800m national champion Navasky Anderson are among those set to their first entry at the 2026 Commonwealth Games.

Former national champion Rohan Watson advanced to Tuesday’s semi-final of the men’s 100m after he won his first round race in 10.13 (1.5m/s).

In the semi-final he is to be joined by Ackeem Blake who drew a bye.

Also advancing were the Ghanaian pair of Benjamin Azamati and Abdul-Rasheed Saminu, as well as Jeremiah Azu of Wales and Favour Ashe of Nigeria.

Both Jamaican entries in the female 100m, Jonielle Smith and Jodean Williams, both of whom had byes, will join the action in the semi-finals.

Former World Athletics champion Tajay Gayle led the qualifying for Wednesday’s final of the men’s long jump with 8.10m (0.1m/s). He is to be joined by Jordan Turner who had a wind-aided 7.84m (4.2m/s).

Gayle, who have won medals at the last two major global championships, had a wind-aided 7.73m (3.3m/s) and 7.40m (1.0m/s) before his big mark.

Turner was was third in his group, behind Indian Sreeshankar’s effort of 8.01m (2.0m/s) and Australian Christopher Mitrevski’s mark of 7.89m (1.8m/s).

National champion Kelly Ann Beckford (2:01.63 minutes) and Adelle Tracey (2:02.58) advanced to Wednesday’s semi-finals of the women’s 800m.

Beckford booked an automatic spot after placing third in her first-round heat behind pre-championships favourite Lillian Odira of Kenya who ran 2:01.05. Isabelle Boffey of Wales clocked 2:01.53.

Tracey advanced on time after she was fourth in her first round race, just outside the automatic qualifying places. Australia’s Sarah Billings won with 2:01.51, followed by Botswana’s Oratile Nowe (2:02.11) and Kenya’s Janet Jepkemoi (2:02.30).

Nayoka Clunis qualified for Tuesday’s women’s hammer throw final, her first major global final. She threw 64.84m in the third round, eighth best of the day.

Distin could be pushed hard in her title defence with the likes of the in-form Australian pair of Eleanor Patterson and Nicola Olyslagers, as well as former NCAA champion Temitope Simbiat Adeshina of Nigeria all ranked ahead of her going into the championships.

The Sweden-based Distin has had a season’s best 1.96m, set indoors in February and has cleared 1.94m outdoors.

Navasky Anderson will be hoping to get back to the final of the men’s 800m after he finished fifth four years ago in Birmingham, England.

Since shocking the track and field world with his gold medal in the men’s 400m in Hungary in 2023, Watson has been through some lean years, failing to get past the semis in Tokyo, Japan, last year. But he has been improving through this season.

Watson will be accompanied by Delano Kennedy and Zandrion Barnes as they seek places in the men’s 400m semi-finals.

Leah Anderson and Shana Kaye Anderson are to line up in the women’s 400m first round.

World.title: Wedding Content Creators
World.content:
A wedding content creator documents your day as it unfolds, using a smartphone to capture raw, candid moments.

Not long ago, every wedding media team consisted of a photographer and videographer. Today, there’s a new professional joining the line-up — the wedding content creator.

If you’ve spent any time on Instagram or TikTok, you’ve probably seen the rise of behind-the-scenes wedding clips, emotional first looks, candid bridal party moments, and beautifully edited reels appearing within hours of the celebration. That’s the work of a wedding content creator.

This person is responsible for capturing authentic, real-time moments throughout the day, usually using a smartphone. The focus isn’t producing a cinematic wedding film or a gallery of professionally edited images. Instead, the wedding content creator documents the experience as it unfolds, creating vertical videos, candid clips, and social-ready content that couples can relive and share almost immediately.

So how are they different from a videographer? A videographer tells the story of your wedding through carefully planned shots, professional cameras, audio equipment, lighting, and expert editing. The result is a timeless wedding film that beautifully documents your ceremony, speeches, and celebration.

A content creator, on the other hand, captures the moments in-between — the laughter while getting ready, your mother’s emotional reaction as she helps you into your dress, the bridesmaids dancing in the suite, your guests’ excitement before the ceremony, or your partner’s nervous smile just before walking down the aisle. These are often the unscripted moments that couples cherish most because they reflect how the day actually felt.

Each has its advantages. A videographer delivers polished, high-quality storytelling that you’ll treasure for decades. The downside is that editing takes time, so your finished film may not arrive for several weeks or even months.

A content creator provides immediate gratification. Many deliver raw footage within 24 hours and edited reels shortly after, allowing couples to relive their day while the emotions are still fresh. However, smartphone footage is not intended to replace the production quality of professional videography.

If your budget allows, having both is the ideal combination.

The videographer preserves your wedding as a timeless film, while the content creator documents the emotion, spontaneity, and behind-the-scenes memories that often never make it into the final edit. Together, they create a complete story — one that is beautifully produced and deeply personal.

If you must choose one, let your priorities guide the decision. If preserving your vows, speeches, and ceremony in cinematic quality is more important, invest in a professional videographer. If you value candid moments, quick delivery, and social-media-ready memories, a content creator may be the better fit.

Whichever you choose, remember that great wedding content isn’t about following trends or chasing viral moments. The best professionals take the time to understand your personalities, your priorities, and the atmosphere you want to create. They know when to step in for a memorable shot and, just as importantly, when to step back and quietly capture the genuine interactions unfolding around them.

Because the most meaningful wedding memories aren’t always the ones you planned. They’re the fleeting glances, unexpected laughter, happy tears, and quiet moments that happen in-between.

At the end of the day, strong wedding content isn’t simply about documenting what happened, it’s about preserving how your wedding day felt — and that’s a memory worth investing in.

World.title: Public Advisory: Fraudulent Website Alert
World.content:
Jamaica Observer Limited is advising the public of an unauthorised and deceptive website that is unlawfully using our name, logo, and other brand elements to imitate our official platform and mislead individuals.

We are aware that a fabricated article is being circulated on social media claiming to originate from the Jamaica Observer.

The article references former Cabinet minister Lisa Hanna and a purported investment platform, and it improperly uses the image and likeness of the public figure, purporting to create the appearance of an endorsement or affiliation with the platform described in the article. No such article was published by the Jamaica Observer, and no such association exists.

These claims are entirely false. The website and related social media posts are fraudulent and have no connection to the Jamaica Observer. Such platforms may attempt to collect personal information, solicit payments, or otherwise misrepresent our services. We urge the public to remain vigilant and ensure they are engaging only with our legitimate channels.

How to Protect Yourself

• Access our official website only: https://www.jamaicaobserver.com/

• Follow our verified social media accounts: https://www.instagram.com/jamaicaobserver/; https://x.com/JamaicaObserver; https://www.youtube.com/@JamaicaObserverJa

• Be cautious of pages or profiles requesting personal information, payments, or unusual engagement

• Report suspicious websites or accounts to the relevant platform and notify us at abuse@jamaicaobserver.com

Jamaica Observer takes the misuse of our brand and intellectual property seriously. We are actively collaborating with the appropriate authorities and digital platforms to remove these fraudulent pages and safeguard the public.

Your trust and safety remain our highest priority.

World.title: We might be in an AI bubble, global finance watchdog chief says
World.content:
"It does look like some of the valuations ... are quite up for the markets overall and for some of these companies. But I'm not a stock market prognosticator. I can't tell you how much further they'll go, whether they're justified or not. But it is something we monitor and discuss and work on trying to make sure that things don't go badly,” Schindler said.

The "central bank for central banks," the Bank for International Settlements, warned that disappointing returns for the AI hyperscalers could result in a "protracted investment bust" which could trigger a "sudden pullback in financing." The International Monetary Fund also warned that markets could contract if AI doesn’t match expectations around its profitability and the productivity gains it can deliver.

The chair of the FSB, Schindler's colleague Andrew Bailey, who is also the Bank of England governor, has cautioned on several occasions of a potential price correction in AI stocks.

But Schindler played down the wider risks, saying: “Our job is to think about all the things that can go wrong and think about ways to make those better. So this is just one of the things.”

Asked whether the finance industry has enough safeguards in place to remain stable if an AI bubble unravels, Schindler said: “I do hope so.”

Banks have “largely proven pretty resilient to shocks” since the 2008 crisis, but the financial system is “always evolving,” he said. Schindler also pointed to the nonbank sector, which is far bigger than it was in 2008 and less regulated than the banking industry.

World.title: Charleroi airport to halt flights in 2028 for over 2 months
World.content:
Brussels South Charleroi Airport , pictured here in March, 2023, is set to be closed for 11 weeks. | Virginie Lefour/Belga Mag/AFP via Getty Images

The suspension is necessary to allow major reconstruction works on the hub’s only runway.

BRUSSELS — Brussels South Charleroi Airport will suspend all flight operations in the second half of 2028 to allow a major reconstruction of its only runway and other infrastructure upgrades.

Belgium's second-busiest airport is expected to halt air traffic for 11 weeks, from Aug. 15 to Oct. 31.

“A complete refurbishment of Charleroi airport's sole runway (which has an estimated lifespan of 25 years), together with other major infrastructure modernisation works, has been scheduled by [airport infrastructure company] SOWAER for the second half of 2028,” the airport said in an email.

World.title: UK Green leader reported to police over Farage guillotine post
World.content:
In a statement, Zia Yusuf, Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, said: “Zack Polanski has posted to his 713k Instagram followers a photo of a man in a T-shirt depicting the beheading of Nigel Farage.

“To do this just 2 weeks after our friend Ann was murdered is staggering. This is incitement to murder. It should be treated as such by the police,” he said.

Ann Widdecombe, a former Tory minister who was Reform UK’s justice spokesperson, was found dead in her home in Devon earlier this month. Joshua Kerry, a 28-year-old man, was charged with her murder last week.

Sharing a screenshot, Nigel Farage wrote on X: “If I was to post anything as inciteful then I would expect to be arrested, and so should Polanski.”

A Green spokesperson said: “Zack condemns the image on the T-shirt. He was tagged in a post with 20 images and clicked accept without realizing there was more to it than he had seen.”

The spokesperson added that the t-shirt is in poor taste, and said the Greens call on everyone involved in public discourse “to show kindness and not encourage more division.”

The Met Police said Monday they had received a third-party report relating to an image shared on social media.

“We take reports of this nature extremely seriously, and officers are conducting enquiries into the matter.”

World.title: US kicks off review of its force posture in Europe
World.content:
U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth arrives to welcome defense ministers from the Baltic states at the Pentagon on July 25, 2025. | Win McNamee/Getty Images

The six-month review was first announced by U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in June during a NATO ministerial meeting.

The United States on Tuesday launched the country's Europe posture review that will determine the number of American troops and military assets on the continent, a top U.S. defense official said.

"This will be a real review, designed to ensure that NATO is moving fast and irreversibly toward Europe taking primary responsibility for its conventional defense," U.S. Undersecretary for Defense Elbridge Colby posted on X.

The six-month review was first announced by U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in June during a NATO ministerial meeting.

World.title: Can Europe fight fires this big?
World.content:
Wildfires raging across France and Spain have forced more than 300,000 people from their homes and stretched national firefighting services to their limits. Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart look at how the EU is helping through its Civil Protection Mechanism and rescEU emergency reserve — and why Brussels says that even dozens more firefighting planes would not be enough without much greater investment in prevention.

Then, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy heads to Washington amid signs that U.S. President Donald Trump and parts of the MAGA movement may be warming towards Kyiv. But will the apparent change of heart translate into sanctions against Russia and concrete military support?

Plus: Could antibodies produced by llamas provide farmers with a safer alternative to chemical pesticides?

World.title: Polanski’s Greens brace for the ‘Burnham bounce’
World.content:
An opinion poll by More in Common published Monday put Labour on top for the first time since March 2025, with its surge coming at the expense of the Greens, who recorded their lowest share of the vote since October last year when Polanski became leader. A separate YouGov poll also released Monday showed no change from last week, though it noted the party is down eight points from a February peak.

Polanski insists he is the “opposite of worried about Andy Burnham,” predicting Labour MPs’ “last roll of the dice” in switching leader won’t improve things.

But a senior Green Party local politician, granted anonymity to speak frankly, acknowledged: “It’s going to be difficult, there is going to be a Burnham bounce,” warning the party needs to “sharpen those key lines that give us differentiation.”

The party is already attacking Burnham for employing corporate lobbyists like his chief of staff James Purnell, and claiming the new prime minister’s rhetoric on Gaza, public ownership and homelessness is hollow, and does not represent a change from Starmer.

It is also on a drive to find more polished spokespeople to hit the airwaves.

Drawing the battle lines

One area where the Greens see a dividing line with Burnham is over Gaza.

World.title: Devastating wildfires expose Europe’s fragile response to a new climate reality
World.content:
European, national and regional authorities are battling another wave of devastating wildfires this summer, but the scale and frequency of extreme weather events are raising questions over whether Europe’s crisis management systems are adapting fast enough, with a rising political cost for responsible administrations and climate deniers.

 

In recent days, Spain and France have been hit by some of the most severe fires of the season. In Spain, wildfires have affected more than 80,000 hectares, while France has seen more than 40,000 hectares burned. Hundreds of thousands of people have been forced to evacuate their homes as flames spread across several regions.

“Europe stands alongside France and Spain in the face of the devastating wildfires ravaging them,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X. “My thoughts are with the firefighters who bravely battle the flames and with all those evacuated.”

Brussels quickly activated the EU Civil Protection Mechanism, deploying firefighting aircraft and personnel from several European countries.

France received support from Czechia, Croatia, Germany, Portugal, Slovakia, Sweden and Türkiye, while Spain received additional aircraft from Greece, Italy and Türkiye. Portugal also sent personnel and vehicles to support the response in Spain.

But behind the immediate response effort lies a broader challenge: Europe's wildfire season seems to be changing faster than its emergency response systems.

At a technical briefing with journalists on Monday, European Commission officials acknowledged that simultaneous large-scale fires across several countries are putting increasing pressure on Europe’s common disaster response capacity and highlighted the need to further strengthen preparedness.

“This is the chronicle of a situation long foretold,” said Juli Pausas, a research professor at the Centre for Research on Desertification in Valencia. “Once we, as a society, have accepted that we are changing the climate, these fires become part of the new normal; in other words, they are exactly what we expected.”

A more intense fire season

Wildfires are not new in southern Europe, but climate change is altering the conditions in which they occur.

The European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (JRC), in its assessment of the 2025 wildfire season, identified a clear trend towards “an earlier start, more frequent and intense heat waves, and fires reaching higher latitudes than historically observed.”

The JRC also found that the traditional wildfire season, historically concentrated between June and September, is expanding, with major fires occurring both earlier in spring and later in the year.

Brussels has attempted to anticipate this growing risk. Last year, the Commission presented a preparedness strategy focused on strengthening early warning systems, improving coordination between national authorities and reinforcing the EU Civil Protection Mechanism.

In June, the Commission announced its largest-ever pre-positioning of firefighting resources, with 777 firefighters deployed in high-risk areas across southern Europe through the European Civil Protection Pool.

“When every minute counts, being prepared saves lives, protects livelihoods, and preserves our environment,” European Commissioner for Equality, Preparedness and Crisis Management Hadja Lahbib said while presenting the plan.

However, the scale of this summer’s fires has renewed calls for further investment. As wildfires continue to spread in other vulnerable regions, including parts of southern Italy, concerns are growing about whether Europe has enough resources if several major emergencies occur simultaneously.

On Tuesday, MEP Georgia Tramacere (S&D/Italy) called for an emergency meeting of member states most affected by wildfires, arguing that governments should share lessons learned and discuss how to strengthen prevention and crisis management.

Spain’s political battle over prevention

In Spain, the fires have triggered a political confrontation between the central government led by the centre-left Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) and regional authorities governed by the centre-right Popular Party (PP).

The most visible clash involved Isabel Díaz Ayuso, president of the Madrid region, and Transport Minister Óscar Puente after Madrid requested national emergency status.

Puente accused PP-led authorities of reducing fire prevention efforts and criticised agreements with the far-right Vox party, which has frequently questioned the severity of climate change. Ayuso dismissed the accusations as political attacks.

The dispute reflects a wider question over responsibility. In Spain, regional governments are responsible for forest management and many emergency services, while the central government coordinates national support and international assistance.

As extreme weather events become more frequent, climate policy is becoming an increasingly sensitive political issue.

“Governing with denialists is to leave the population unprotected,” Ecological Transition Minister Sara Aagesen told reporters on Monday.

France faces scrutiny over preparedness

France has also faced political pressure following major fires in the south-west, including the Gironde region near Bordeaux.

President Emmanuel Macron mobilised additional resources as the fires spread, while the government held several interministerial crisis meetings.

“The fight against wildfires begins with prevention. Nine out of ten fires are human-caused, and most arise from carelessness,” Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu wrote on X. He also warned that some fires appeared to have been deliberately started.

Beyond the immediate response, the fires have revived a debate over whether France has invested enough in prevention and firefighting capacity.

Manuel Bompard, national coordinator of the far-left party La France Insoumise, criticised the previous government led by Gabriel Attal, claiming that cuts to civil protection funding contributed to delays in renewing two firefighting aircraft.

The far-right National Rally has also faced scrutiny, with opponents accusing the party of publicly supporting firefighters while opposing measures to strengthen their resources in the National Assembly.

Wildfires as a political issue

Across Europe, wildfires are becoming a test of whether national governments and local authorities can adapt their response to a changing climate.

In the EU, the challenge is no longer only responding to individual disasters, but ensuring that Europe has enough shared capacity when several crises unfold simultaneously.

Politically, the costs are likely to fall on public authorities that are struggling to keep pace with a rapidly changing reality, as well as on right-wing parties that have made climate change denial a central part of their political identity.

World.title: French wildfires threaten defence sites and hit regional economy
World.content:
Wildfires in France’s south-western Gironde department have forced evacuations and protective measures at strategically important defence and aerospace sites around Bordeaux, disrupting one of the country’s most important industrial clusters.

 

Among the affected companies are ArianeGroup, Dassault Aviation, Airbus Atlantic and missile-propulsion specialist Roxel.

The French Defence Ministry said 1,500 military personnel had been deployed since Saturday to support the emergency response. It added that “experts and resources” had been sent to help secure industrial sites in coordination with other government departments.

ArianeGroup, whose facilities in the area produce propulsion systems for Europe’s Ariane rockets and France’s M51 ballistic missiles, told AFP on Monday that the firm is in constant contact with both local and national authorities. The issues related to the protection of ArianeGroup sites are being addressed," the company told AFP.

French media TF1 reported that Roxel, a subsidiary of European missile manufacturer MBDA, operates at the high-risk industrial complex in Saint-Médard-en-Jalles, where it produces solid-propellant systems for tactical missiles. A few kilometres away, complexes belonging to Dassault, Safran, and Thales also appear vulnerable. Roxel told Le Monde that the necessary measures had been taken to protect its operations and employees, with support from the authorities.

According to Defense News, Dassault Aviation was working with France’s Directorate General of Armaments and the prefectural authorities, as it had transferred sensitive equipment from its Martignas plant and Cestas logistics centre to its Mérignac site and nearby Air Base 106.

The company also told AFP that most employees at its Mérignac and Martignas facilities were remaining at home. Dassault’s Mérignac facility handles the final assembly and flight testing of Rafale fighter aircraft and Falcon business jets, while its Martignas plant specialises in aerostructures.

Airbus Atlantic also evacuated employees from its Salaunes facility at the authorities’ request. The site produces fuselage components for Airbus A220 and A350 aircraft.

An ‘economic thunderbolt’

The disruption to strategic industry is part of a much broader economic shock across Gironde.

Since breaking out on 22 July, the fire has burned across approximately 42,000 hectares, prompted the evacuation of around 220,000 people and destroyed about 240 homes, according to the latest official figures.

The blaze remained “stabilised” on Tuesday morning after a relatively calm night, according to the Gironde prefecture. Officials nevertheless warned that rising temperatures and lower humidity could cause conditions to deteriorate again.

More than 13,000 businesses are located in Gironde’s evacuation zones, including approximately 7,000 craft businesses and 6,300 retailers, according to France’s Economy Ministry. They have been unable to operate normally because of evacuation orders.

The Bordeaux-Gironde Chamber of Commerce and Industry estimates that around 130,000 employees have been prevented from working normally.

Economy Minister Roland Lescure described the fires as an “economic thunderbolt affecting a region that did not need it”.

Carsten Brzeski, ING’s global head of macroeconomics, said the overall economic impact “should become measurable”, pointing to lost working hours, lower productivity and disruption to logistics.

The French government announced emergency support on Monday for businesses affected by fires in Gironde, the Landes and the Var. Companies in evacuation zones will be able to use the state-supported partial-unemployment scheme.

France Assureurs also extended the deadline for submitting claims until 31 August.

A meeting will be held at the Economy Ministry on Thursday to provide “more precise answers” to affected companies, Industry Minister Sébastien Martin told BFMTV-RMC.

Tourism, forestry and wine face losses

Tourism businesses face cancellations and closures during what should have been one of their busiest periods of the year. Companies across the affected area are also reporting spoiled stock, interrupted supply chains and employee absences.

The fire is also disrupting activity in the Landes de Gascogne forest, one of the main centres of France’s commercial timber industry.

The timber sector is the third-largest industrial sector in Nouvelle-Aquitaine. It supports approximately 56,000 jobs, including around 34,000 connected with the Landes de Gascogne forest, and generates an estimated €10 billion in annual revenue.

Bordeaux’s vineyards had escaped direct fire damage as of 27 July, according to Le Monde. Winemakers nevertheless warned that smoke could taint grapes and affect the quality of forthcoming vintages.

The cost extends beyond insured damage

The eventual economic cost is likely to extend far beyond visible destruction and the losses covered by insurers.

According to Allianz Research, only around 10% of European economic losses from heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and other climatological events were insured between 1980 and 2022. By comparison, more than one-third of losses caused by storms, hail and wind were insured.

These calculations cover only direct damage to assets. They exclude deaths, healthcare expenditure and lost productivity, which can represent a substantial part of the cost of heatwaves and wildfires.

A study published in Nature Sustainability estimated that California’s 2018 wildfires caused $148.5 billion in total damage. Direct capital destruction represented 19% of that figure, while health costs accounted for 22% and indirect economic disruption for 59%.

The study found that supply-chain effects spread far beyond the burned areas, with more than half of the indirect losses occurring outside California.

The European Central Bank separately estimates that only around one-quarter of climate-related catastrophe losses in the EU were insured between 1980 and 2023.

Insurance Europe puts the average protection gap — the proportion of losses left uninsured — at 53% in France and 60% in Spain between 2015 and 2024, based on Munich Re data.

“With the wildfires, the bittersweet consequence, as with other natural disasters, is that it will actually lead to positive economic activity once the rebuilding starts,” Brzeski said.

However, he added that households, insurers and the government would ultimately have to bear the cost of reconstruction.

With temperatures forecast to rise again this week, businesses and industrial operators face the prospect that evacuations and production interruptions could be extended.

World.title: Europe is burning : How bad could this wildfire crisis get?
World.content:
Europe is facing one of its worst wildfire seasons in years, with France and Spain bearing the brunt of large, fast-moving blazes fuelled by repeated heatwaves, drought and strong winds.

 

Thousands of firefighters are battling fires that have forced mass evacuations, destroyed tens of thousands of hectares of forest and disrupted tourism during the peak summer season.

Portugal, Greece, Italy, Turkey and parts of the Western Balkans are also at risk due to expected rising temperatures.

Euronews has examined the latest wildfire trends, the factors driving their spread and the challenges Europe faces in preventing future disasters.

Where are the wildfires hitting the most?

Active since 22 July, wildfires are currently concentrated in southwestern France as well as in central and eastern Spain.

The worst-affected areas include western Madrid, where authorities are tackling one of the region’s largest fires on record, as well as Ávila, Toledo and Castellón on Spain’s eastern coast, where an uncontrolled blaze is still burning.

"The scale of the disaster we are living through is very hard to accept," said Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on 26 July.

In France, the Gironde region around Bordeaux is Europe's biggest wildfire hotspot. French authorities have described it as the country's worst wildfire emergency in decades, with President Emmanuel Macron calling it the worst since World War II.

"In Gironde, we are continuing to fight. The fire has been stabilised, as we say, but it remains very intense... We are doing everything we can to stop it," Macron told reporters.

What has been destroyed so far?

The destruction has been extensive and is still being assessed as fires continue to burn. So far, at least 80,000 hectares have been lost to the fires in Spain and 42,000 in France.

Two firefighters died in France and another died in Italy while working to tackle wildfires.

At least 240 homes have been completely destroyed, with many more damaged, near Bordeaux, in Le Porge.

More than 320,000 people have been evacuated across Spain and France. In France, authorities ordered nearly 4,000 additional residents and tourists to leave coastal areas along the Atlantic on Tuesday as a precautionary measure.

How is the European Union helping?

The European Union's main tool is the EU Civil Protection Mechanism (EUCPM), a solidarity system through which member states and participating countries share firefighting resources when national capacities are overwhelmed.

When a country requests assistance, the European Commission's Emergency Response Coordination Centre (ERCCC) coordinates offers of aircraft, helicopters and firefighting teams from across Europe, as well as co-financing their transport and, in some cases, operational costs.

For this wildfire season, the European Commission, through its rescEU mechanism linked to the EUCPM maintains a transitional firefighting fleet of 22 aircraft and five helicopters, which can be deployed to countries facing major fires.

The Commission deployed more than 770 firefighters from 14 countries across high-risk areas in Portugal, Spain, France, Italy, Greece and Cyprus to improve preparedness and facilitate the exchange of firefighting expertise.

It also created a dedicated Wildfire Support Team within the ERCC to monitor wildfire risks around the clock and coordinate responses during the fire season.

So far, the EU's civil mechanism supported France with two small Air Tractor firefighting planes from Portugal, one Black Hawk helicopter from Slovakia and another one from Czechia which arrived at the Bordeaux-Mérignac airport on 24 July.

One Croatian Canadair firefighting plane arrived in Nîmes on 24 July, followed by two Swedish water-scooping planes and a technical team in Bordeaux-Mérignac on 25 July. A European Commission liaison officer was deployed to Bordeaux on 24 July.

The EU's Copernicus service is also providing emergency satellite maps of the affected areas.

Spain received two Greek and two Italian Canadair firefighting planes in Torrejón de Ardoz on 25 July, along with two Turkish Air Tractor planes and three Portuguese ground firefighting teams (134 personnel, 41 vehicles) in Burgohondo.

Two helicopters were due to be deployed on Tuesday from Germany as well as two additional planes from Türkiye.

How much worse can it get?

Europe has experienced three major heatwaves this summer, leaving vegetation exceptionally dry.

Another spell of high temperatures is forecast this week, raising concerns that new fires could ignite and existing ones could spread rapidly.

Although authorities in Gironde and Nouvelle-Aquitaine said the wildfire, which has ravaged 42,000 hectares of vegetation in less than a week, remained “contained” on Tuesday, they warned that weather conditions were expected to remain unfavourable, particularly due to rising temperatures, according to French newspaper Le Monde.

Portugal, Greece, Italy, Turkey and parts of the Western Balkans are also at risk due to the expected rising temperatures.

Related France and Spain battle to control wildfires ahead of expected heatwave

However, Commission officials said that emergency response alone will not be enough as climate change makes wildfires larger and more intense.

During a private briefing, they argued that Europe needs an integrated management approach, combining firefighting with prevention measures such as better forest management and reducing combustible vegetation in landscapes to lower the risk and intensity of future fires.

Scientists said the combination of prolonged heat and drought has created ideal wildfire conditions across southern Europe.

Are humans responsible?

While the extreme weather conditions driving the fires are strongly linked to climate change, many individual wildfires are still started by human activity.

According to the Commission, around 96% of wildfires in Europe are caused by human activity, either accidentally or deliberately. Causes could range from discarded cigarettes, barbecues and campfires to sparks from machinery, power lines or arson.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez stated recently that nine out of ten wildfires are caused by human activity, with over 110 suspected arsonists arrested nationwide amid severe summer blazes.

In Portugal, arson was the cause of 84% of the area burned in 2024, with estimated damage to the forest at €67 million, according to official data.

World.title: Zinedine Zidane fulfils 'dream' as he takes charge of France
World.content:
Zinedine Zidane will take charge of France on a four-year contract from 1 August, ending Didier Deschamps' 14-year reign as head coach.

 

“I’m excited,” Zidane said. “The France team makes you dream. We have extraordinary players, an extraordinary team.”

More than 20 years after leaving Les Bleus as a player, Zinedine Zidane is taking over from Didier Deschamps.

The decision was made official on Tuesday by Philippe Diallo, president of the French Football Federation (FFF), who opened the press conference by thanking "DD" for taking the France team "to the very top."

"Zinedine is a legend of French football and for many years he has made it known that one of his dreams was to coach the France team," the head of the FFF said.

Philippe Diallo also revealed the details of the new coach's contract: Zidane will lead Les Bleus for four years, covering the Nations League qualifiers, Euro 2028 and the 2030 World Cup.

"DD is DD, Zizou is Zizou"

Zinedine Zidane began his first address as France head coach with a message of support for those affected by the wildfires in southwestern France, as well as for the firefighters and farmers on the front line.

"That's my first thought," he said.

He also revealed that he had received several offers to manage clubs in recent years but had turned them all down "for the France team."

"For me, it's an immense joy. I don't have any other words," he said.

As for his approach, the 1998 World Cup hero set out a clear objective on Tuesday: "for the France team to keep on winning."

"DD is DD, Blanc was Blanc, Zizou is Zizou. I'm going to do what I know how to do," he told reporters.

The new head coach will officially take up his duties on 1 August. His coaching staff will be unveiled in September, although he indicated it would be "practically" the same as the one that worked with him at Real Madrid.

"I'm pretty loyal on that front," he said.

"We haven't spoken with Kylian"

As for the players, Zidane will announce his first France squad in September. For now, he said he has not spoken to any of them, including captain Kylian Mbappé.

"The most important thing for him is to rest. We'll have the chance to talk about all that soon, in September," he said, without confirming whether the forward will remain captain.

While he said he would explain his "Zinedine Zidane method" at a later stage, the new head coach has already identified Les Bleus' greatest strength: their squad.

"I know we have what it takes. We have extraordinary players. Now I need to see them and explain what I'm going to do," he said.

"Racism has to be fought"

Asked about racist abuse directed at France players after recent matches, Zinedine Zidane called for people to "fight racism."

"We might not change things. We live in a wonderful country with this diversity. I grew up in a neighbourhood where there was room for everyone. That's my life," he said. "Engaging with everyone. That's what we're trying to do."

The new head coach also had a message for supporters in his hometown of Marseille.

"They've always been there, and whenever I return to the region, I feel the passion. I want to keep making them dream."

Didier Deschamps steps down after France's disappointing World Cup exit but leaves behind a remarkable legacy. During his 14 years in charge of Les Bleus, he won the 2018 World Cup, reached the 2022 World Cup final and the 2026 semi-finals, and led France to the Euro 2016 final.

France will play four matches in September, including Zidane's first game in charge away to Turkey on 25 September.

World.title: Marmaris: sailing gulets, ancient ruins and Türkiye's pine honey capital
World.content:
The journey begins at sea, aboard a traditional gullet, a wooden boat still built by hand along this coast, much as it has been for generations. Sailing the famous Blue Voyage, travellers pass the ancient hilltop ruins of Amos before dropping anchor in Kumlubük Bay, where the water is calm and clear enough for snorkelling straight off the boat.

 

But Marmaris's identity doesn't end at the shoreline. Inland, Marmaris National Park's 30,000 hectares of Mediterranean pine forest lead to Nimara Cave, used as shelter by humans since the Palaeolithic age.

Those same forests sustain a local tradition few visitors expect: pine honey, made not from nectar but from honeydew collected on the trees, darker and less sweet than most. At the Marmaris Honey House, that centuries-old craft is on full display, fitting, since Türkiye produces around 92% of the world's pine honey, much of it from this very region.

World.title: Watermarks on the Silk Road: Following Uzbekistan's rivers, waterfalls and ancient reservoirs
World.content:
More than 600 rivers and streams flow across Uzbekistan. Together with around 300 natural and artificial lakes and more than 50 major reservoirs, they supply drinking water, support agriculture and hydropower, and increasingly attract visitors looking to explore the country's diverse landscapes.

 

Water has influenced where people settled, how communities developed and why travellers stopped across what is now Uzbekistan. The Ugam river, the waterfalls of Jizzakh and the historic hovuzs (pools) of Bukhara each tell part of that story. Today, many of these places continue to serve local residents while offering a different way to explore Uzbekistan.

The waterways of the Tashkent region

Just over an hour from Tashkent, the Ugam river flows through the foothills of the Western Tian Shan before continuing into the Bo'stonliq District. Fed by snowmelt and mountain springs, it is one of Uzbekistan's main mountain waterways, supplying nearby communities while supporting local ecosystems and agriculture.

The river has also become one of the region's most popular destinations for outdoor recreation. Recreation areas, swimming pools, restaurants and picnic sites line parts of its banks during the warmer months.

“Along the Ugam river there is a children's playground, various pools, special recreational areas where guests can relax, a restaurant, and facilities where people can prepare their own food,” says Ravshan Temirov.

Further into the mountains, another attraction has developed in the village of Nanay. An irrigation canal originally built to supply household gardens now creates a waterfall that attracts visitors throughout the summer.

According to local guide Dilshod Ashurmetov, the waterfall itself is the result of hashar, the long-standing tradition of voluntary community work that remains common across Uzbekistan.

“This waterfall was created long ago through hashar, community work. We have special vehicles and young men assigned to bring visitors to the waterfall and then take them back. There are tapchans and seating platforms where people can relax, eat food and spend their free time,” he explains.

For local visitor Sabohat Zakirova, the attraction is the peaceful environment around the flowing water.

"My little grandson had a cough. After coming here, his cough went away. We've spent fifteen days relaxing here by the waterfall, and we hope to come again next year,” she says.

Qizilsuv and the springs of Jizzakh

Several hours to the south, the landscape changes. In the mountains of Jizzakh region, natural springs emerge from rocky slopes, feeding streams and waterfalls that continue flowing throughout the year.

"The waterfall you see here is natural. It is formed by springs that gather above and flow down naturally. People living below also use it as drinking water. In winter, this spring water does not freeze," says Jahongir Shukurov, head of division at Baxmal State Forestry.

One of the best-known sites is Qizilsuv waterfall, hidden within the forests of Bakhmal district. Surrounded by rocky cliffs and greenery, it has become increasingly popular with hikers and nature lovers seeking cooler temperatures during the summer months.

Researchers have identified naturally elevated levels of iron in the spring water, while local authorities are considering projects that would expand tourism infrastructure, including camping areas and recreation facilities.

“We conducted research and laboratory analysis, which showed that Qizilsuv contains a high level of iron,” says Akbarjon Qolberdiyev, chief engineer at Bakhmal State Forestry.

He says the area currently receives between 2,000 and 3,000 international visitors each year, alongside between 30,000 and 50,000 domestic tourists.

For many people, however, the attraction is much simpler.

“This is my first time coming to the stream known as Qizilsuv. What I liked most was the cleanliness of the water, its clarity and its softness,” says visitor Nargiza Oqilova.

The reservoirs that sustained Bukhara

Unlike the mountain rivers of eastern Uzbekistan, water in Bukhara had to be collected and stored.

Located on the edge of the Kyzylkum Desert, the city depended on a network of public reservoirs known as hovuzs. They supplied drinking water, supported everyday life and became gathering places where residents could rest beneath the shade of trees during the hottest months of the year.

Among the best preserved is Lyabi Hauz, one of Bukhara's best-known architectural ensembles. Developed during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, it grew around a large stone-lined reservoir that became one of the city's main public spaces. According to local legend, statesman Nadir Divan-Begi financed the construction after selling a valuable jewel he had received during his travels, choosing to leave a public monument for future generations.

Researcher Iskandar Hamroev from Bukhara State University says the reservoirs served far more than one purpose.

“Bukhara is located near the Kyzylkum desert, and the weather is very hot. People came here to rest under the trees. The pools also served as water reserves. Today, people mainly come here to sit and relax,” he says.

Another surviving reservoir, Bolohovuz, stands opposite the Ark fortress. Built in the early eighteenth century during the Ashtarkhanid dynasty, it supplied water to the Emir's residence, government officials and nearby neighbourhoods. Its name comes from the Persian-Tajik words bolo (upper) and hovuz (pool), reflecting its position in the upper part of the historic city.

“Bolohovuz was created because there was a need for water. The residents of the surrounding neighbourhoods also used the water according to their everyday domestic needs,” Hamroev explains.

Although these rivers, waterfalls and reservoirs served different purposes, they share a common role in Uzbekistan's history. They supported settlements, sustained communities and shaped the trade routes that connected people across Central Asia. Today, they continue to offer a different perspective on the country's landscapes, beyond its better-known Silk Road monuments.

World.title: Many feared dead after quake leaves shoppers trapped in Japanese mall
World.content:
The fire department in Japan's Kashima town have released a statement confirming a shopping complex's second floor collapsed, "leaving many people trapped inside", following an earthquake on Tuesday afternoon.

 

According to preliminary measurements, a 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Kumamoto prefecture in southern Japan, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) reported.

One person was killed when a house collapsed, according to Kyodo News.

The agency said the quake began on the seabed off the coast of Kumamoto at a depth of about ten kilometres, triggering a tsunami warning that was lifted shortly afterwards. Around 50 people were taken to hospital. There were no immediate reports of damage.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged the public on the X social media platform to stay away from the coast. She said the government had set up a taskforce to gather information, assess any potential damage and, if necessary, prepare rescue operations.

The Japanese government had earlier issued warnings for the affected areas, including the prefectures of Kumamoto, Nagasaki, Kagoshima, Fukuoka, Saga, Oita and Miyazaki on the island of Kyushu. Authorities urged around 150,000 people to seek refuge in shelters specifically designated for earthquakes.

The quake left at least 48,000 households without electricity on Kyushu, and rail services were suspended, with Shinkansen bullet trains also halted.

Areas affected by the earthquake in southern Japan Japán meteorológiai szolgálat (JMA)

Japan's Nuclear Regulation Authority said no irregularities had been detected at three nuclear power plants close to the quake.

The strong tremor was also felt in parts of South Korea, including the major south-eastern port city of Busan.

The area has a history of quakes; 10 years ago, a powerful earthquake in Kumamoto claimed 275 lives, injured 2,739 people and left tens of thousands of residents homeless.

World.title: EU civil protection mechanism: coordinating Europe's firefighters
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron has activated the EU civil protection mechanism to help combat devastating wildfires. The system has become increasingly effective, yet it will reach its limits in the summer of 2026.

France is quite well-prepared for wildfires. The government operates 12 Canadair water bombers and eight Dash firefighting aircraft. In addition, leased aircraft and helicopters are being used.

However, the fleet is currently needed simultaneously across many parts of the country. A drought has been intensifying for weeks, and several heat waves with temperatures sometimes exceeding 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) have left the vegetation extremely parched. The devastating wildfire near Bordeaux on the Atlantic coast has already engulfed more than 42,000 hectares of forest and vegetation.

At the same time, fires and follow-up extinguishing efforts in southern and southeastern France are tying up additional emergency personnel. In many places, firefighters are battling the flames in an exhausting, round-the-clock effort. However, strong winds are fanning the fire fronts, making them almost unstoppable, and more than 220,000 people have had to leave their homes and vacation homes so far.

The gravity of the situation is also underscored by the fact that the French government has deployed an A400M military transport aircraft equipped for aerial firefighting for the first time. The A400M can drop around 20 metric tons of fire retardant, more than three times as much as a Canadair.

Nevertheless, the situation is currently so dire that President Emmanuel Macron also activated the EU civil protection mechanism (CPM) and requested assistance from other European countries.

The French Air Force military transport A400M aircraft makes its first-ever drop of fire retardant Image: Abdul Saboor/AFP

24/7 service at the emergency response coordination centre

To activate the CPM, a country reports its needs to the European Union's emergency response coordination centre, ERCC, in Brussels. ERCC experts assess which of the 37 participating countries can provide assistance.

Initial assistance for France was mobilized within a few hours and has since been significantly expanded. Firefighting aircraft and helicopters from Portugal, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Germany, Turkey, Sweden and Slovakia are supporting France, primarily in the greater Bordeaux area.

At the same time, however, the EU also dispatched six additional firefighting aircraft from Greece, Turkey and Italy to Spain. This means that 13 of the 22 firefighting aircraft available for this summer have already been mobilized for these two countries. The figures also demonstrate how quickly the European reserve can be drawn upon when multiple large-scale wildfires occur simultaneously. According to the European Commission, the resources currently available are therefore likely insufficient to keep pace with the scale of the fires.

Turkey, Norway and others cooperate with EU members

Since the launch of the civil protection mechanism in 2001, the system has been expanded several times. Since 2019, the EU has also launched rescEU, a strategic reserve comprising firefighting aircraft, medical equipment, field hospitals and specialized technology for chemical or nuclear emergencies. In addition to the 27 EU member states, 10 other countries are also participating in the civil protection mechanism, including Norway, Turkey and several Western Balkan states.

For the summer of 2026, Brussels also pre-positioned 777 firefighters from 14 countries in particularly vulnerable regions of France, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece and Cyprus. The firefighting aircraft and helicopters of the European reserve are distributed across twelve countries and can be mobilized through the coordination center in Brussels. In addition, firefighting efforts are supported by high-resolution satellite imagery from the EU's Copernicus Earth observation program.

The heart of this cooperation is that one country may be able to spare aircraft or emergency personnel while another urgently needs them. However, the European principle of solidarity reaches its limits in situations where multiple countries are simultaneously affected by extreme weather events, which are likely to occur with increasing frequency due to climate change. In such cases, governments must weigh how much support they can send abroad without jeopardizing their own operational capacity.

Currently, Italy is battling wildfires within its own borders, even though it has not yet activated the mechanism. The European Commission expects an unusually long wildfire season this year. The mechanism was first activated at the end of April and could remain in effect until as late as early November.

Even the sky glows deep red over Lake Moutchic as the Lege-Cap-Ferret wildfire illuminates the horizon in Gironde, France Image: Fabrice Sapte/ABACAPRESS/IMAGO

Plans for a separate 'EU firefighting fleet'

The current European air reserve for fighting wildfires consists primarily of nationally operated aircraft that are committed as EU resources for a specific period. Meanwhile, the EU is establishing a rescEU fleet — permanently available and fully funded by EU resources — at a cost of approximately €600 million ($682m).

The plan is to acquire twelve new firefighting aircraft, which will be stationed in France, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece and Croatia. The aircraft will be operated by the respective member states, but decisions regarding their deployment within the rescEU framework will be made jointly by the European Commission and the participating countries.

France owns several Canadair aircraft but needed to request help from abroad in fighting the current wildfires Image: Thomas Samson/AFP

Wildfire prevention is key

Europe's wildfire response force can save time in an emergency and relieve the strain on national disaster response teams. However, according to the European Commission, this cannot compensate for a lack of wildfire prevention measures such as the creation of firebreaks and stricter building regulations in high-risk areas.

Furthermore, firefighting aircraft are most effective when fires are detected early. Once fire fronts measuring several kilometers have formed due to heat and strong winds, even additional aircraft from the European Union can often only contain the flames, but not fully extinguish them.

World.title: Poland: Top court rejects recognizing EU same-sex marriages
World.content:
Poland's constitutional court has overturned plans to recognize same-sex marriages that took place in other EU member states. This defies an order from the EU's top court and could set up a clash on the matter.

Poland's highest court, the Constitutional Tribunal on Tuesday overturned a law that would have led to the legal recognition of same-sex spouses who married in other EU member states and subsequently moved to Poland.

The government in Warsaw had been moving to accommodate a ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union saying that majority-Catholic Poland, which does not permit same-sex marriage domestically, must at least recognize unions contracted elsewhere in the EU.

The unanimous ruling could set up a power struggle between Poland's top court and that of the 27-member bloc.

What did Poland's Constitutional Tribunal rule?

The court said in a statement on Tuesday that the judgment was unanimous and final and that EU same-sex marriages could not be copied into the country's civil registry as previously planned.

It said that the plans for the "preparation and issuance of certified copies concerning unions contracted abroad that do not constitute a union between a woman and a man," were "inconsistent with Article 92, Paragraph 1, in conjunction with Article 18 of the Constitution of the Republic of Poland."

Article 18 of the constitution reads as follows: "Marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, as well as the family, motherhood and parenthood, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland."

In other words it both designates marriage as heterosexual in nature and as part of Poland's jurisdiction.

Article 92, Paragraph 1 meanwhile specifies that regulations should be specified by "the organs specified in the Constitution."

The court did not elaborate on its reasoning in its short statement, but this seemed to suggest its judges found that the European court order encroached on Poland's authority to set its family and marriage policies.

Poland: Have things improved for the LGBTQ+ community? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What had been previously agreed, when, and why?

The November 2025 ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union had not demanded that Poland legalize gay marriage, nor even that it recognize same-sex spouses as such legally.

It did, however, demand that a same-sex couple who married legally elsewhere in the EU and then exercised "their freedom of movement to move and reside" in another state, like Poland, should have their marital status copied into the civil register if that was the only way to secure the benefits and securities of marital status in that country.

The case was initiated by two men, a Polish national and a German-Polish dual national, who had married legally while living in Germany in 2018 and then moved to Poland the following year.

Poland's Supreme Administrative Court had ruled in March that this step "does not violate national identity," nor interfere with Poland's authority to determine its own family and marriage laws.

Poland's government subsequently implemented the legislation in May, and it had been set to come into force as of the end of August.

But the right-wing opposition PiS party challenged the move at the Constitutional Tribunal, successfully as it transpires.

Poland's Constitutional Tribunal and the top EU courts have clashed before, not least in a long-running dispute over the contentious appointment of new judges to the court when PiS was in government, with the most recent European Court of Justice rebuke of Poland's top court being issued last December.

Poland, with roughly 70% of the population identifying as Roman Catholic in census data, is one of just four EU members not to permit either same-sex marriages or same-sex civil unions, along with Bulgaria, Romania and Slovakia.
