World.title: Timișoara City Celebration expands accessibility with sign language concerts, inclusive spaces
World.content:
This year's Timișoara City Celebration will expand accessibility measures for people with hearing impairments and neurodiverse visitors, with sign language interpretation at several headline concerts and dedicated viewing areas. The event will take place between July 31 and August 3.

The organizers said concerts by Beth Hart, The Script, Irina Rimes, and Alexandra Căpitănescu will be interpreted into Romanian Sign Language (LSR), continuing an initiative first introduced during Timișoara's 2023 European Capital of Culture program and maintained in subsequent editions of the festival.

Romanian Sign Language interpretation will be provided by Denis Blidariu, an interpreter who has worked at concerts, festivals, theaters, cinemas, and international conferences.

The main stage area will also include a dedicated viewing platform for neurodiverse visitors, designed to provide a more comfortable concert experience and improved visibility. A separate area will be available for people with hearing impairments.

The accessibility measures are part of a broader effort by the Timișoara Project Center, one of the event's organizers, to make public cultural events more inclusive.

The 2026 edition of Timișoara City Celebration will be held under the theme "One city. A thousand ways to experience it. Diversity.”

World.title: Four bears to be transferred from Romania's Libearty Sanctuary to wildlife park in France
World.content:
Four rescued brown bears from Romania's Libearty Sanctuary in Zărnești will be relocated to a wildlife park in France as part of an international conservation partnership, Agerpres reported. The transfer, involving four young sibling bears, was described by the sanctuary's operator as an unprecedented operation for Romania.

The Millions of Friends Association (AMP), which manages the sanctuary, said the bears, named Alexandra, Anita, Chance, and Thomas, are about two and a half years old and were rescued from the wild.

They will be transported by road to Parc Animalier de Sainte-Croix after being sedated, with the journey expected to take more than a day.

“Four bears rescued from the wild and now in our care will leave Romania together for a park in France. […] It is an unprecedented transfer for AMP Libearty and a unique event for Romania," the association said.

According to AMP, as quoted by the news agency, the relocation has been planned in detail to ensure the animals' safety throughout the journey.

The organization said that the French park shares a similar vision focused on wildlife conservation and environmental education.

Parc Animalier de Sainte-Croix spans 120 hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals from 100 European wildlife species. In addition to its conservation work, the park offers visitors the opportunity to stay overnight in cabins within the park and observe the animals from close range, according to Agerpres.

World.title: IT tops sectors in Romania with highest salaries despite layoffs
World.content:
IT remained the field with the highest salaries on the Romanian market in the first half of 2026, despite the contraction in hiring volumes and even layoffs in profile companies. Salaries in the sector averaged RON 8,000, up by 5% compared to last year, according to Salario data, the salary comparator operated by eJobs.

The second best-paid sector on the market was oil and gas, with a net average of RON 7,000, followed by research and development, at RON 6,800. All three sectors were also featured in the ranking of the best-paying fields last year.

The following industries were construction/installations (RON 6,500) and engineering, telecommunications, audit/consultancy, and naval/aeronautics, each with RON 6,000 net per month on average.

“Even though in most fields we are talking about salary increases compared with last year, in real terms employees’ purchasing power has decreased, including in the sectors where salaries increased the most, because the increases were, in most cases, even half the level of inflation. In June, the inflation rate was 10.4%,” said Roxana Drăghici, Head of Sales at eJobs, the largest online recruitment platform in Romania.

Salario data showed that employees’ expectations exceeded the salaries they received by 30% on average. The largest differences were in IT, where the salary expectations expressed by candidates were 50% higher than those offered by employers. As such, employees in this sector expected an average of RON 11,993.

The insurance sector showed differences of 42%, while the automotive industry, legal and banking sectors showed differences of 40%.

By comparison, employees in the oil and gas sector expected an average salary of RON 9,000, compared to the actual salary average, RON 7,000. In alternative medicine, the difference was only 14%, in sanitary installations 20%, and in customer relations 25%.

Data also showed that among the fields with the lowest salaries are the industries that bring the largest number of jobs to the market, namely retail, services, the food industry, and tourism. The average net salaries for these sectors were RON 4,300 for retail, RON 4,500 for the food industry, RON 4,400 for call-center/BPO, RON 5,000 for transport/logistics, and RON 5,500 for services.

The field with the lowest salaries, however, is au pair/babysitting/cleaning, with RON 3,300 per month.

According to official data, in May the average salary in the Romanian economy reached RON 5,684, up by 3.2% compared with May 2025.

World.title: Revolut opens private market funds to retail investors in Romania
World.content:
Revolut said that it launched access to private market funds for individual investors in Romania, allowing eligible customers to invest in private equity, private credit, and infrastructure assets through its app. The funds are managed by Apollo, Ares, Hamilton Lane, and Partners Group and are structured under the European Union’s ELTIF 2.0 framework.

Private market investments have traditionally been dominated by institutional investors, partly because minimum commitments can exceed EUR 100,000 and because products often involve complex documentation, capital calls, and long lock-up periods.

Revolut said the new offering is aimed at experienced investors with a long-term investment horizon and is intended to lower some of those entry barriers. Management and performance fees may apply.

The four asset managers included in the initial offering collectively manage or oversee more than USD 2.8 trillion in assets, according to the fintech company. Revolut said its internal fund selection team assesses each product’s strategy, performance history, operational resilience, and ability to withstand different market cycles.

“For a long time, private markets have been missing from the average investor’s portfolio, not because of a lack of interest, but because of a lack of access,” said Rolandas Juteika, Revolut’s head of wealth and trading for the European Economic Area. “By partnering with firms such as Apollo, Ares, Hamilton Lane, and Partners Group, we are changing that dynamic.”

The funds will use the ELTIF 2.0 structure, which was designed to broaden access to long-term investments across the EU. The products offered through Revolut will be evergreen funds, meaning investors can put money into an existing portfolio rather than waiting for capital to be deployed gradually.

However, the company warned that the investments remain fundamentally illiquid despite offering periodic redemption windows. Withdrawals are not guaranteed and may be limited or suspended under the terms of each fund.

“These funds are deliberately structured for long-term capital, reflecting the underlying nature of private assets,” Juteika said.

Revolut said investors should be prepared to hold the products for several years and should only allocate a small portion of their overall portfolio to an ELTIF.

World.title: Colombia to close embassy in Romania shortly after reopening it
World.content:
Colombia’s president-elect, Abelardo de la Espriella, announced on Sunday, July 26, that his administration, which will take office on August 7, will close at least 14 embassies, including the one in Romania, as part of a reorganization of the country’s diplomatic network.

Earlier this year, during the mandate of the current president of the South American country, Gustavo Petro, Colombia had reopened its embassy in Romania after 24 years of direct diplomatic absence between the two states.

The new president presented another course regarding the embassies. “In a first stage, I will close the embassies in Algeria, Azerbaijan, Barbados, Cuba, the Czech Republic, Ethiopia, Ghana, Haiti, Hungary, Malaysia, Nicaragua, Romania, Senegal, and South Africa,” De la Espriella said in a speech on his social media accounts in which he also announced the suspension of the opening of the mission in Palestine, according to Euronews English.

De la Espriella assured that these measures “do not mean the severing of diplomatic relations” with the affected countries, except for Cuba and Nicaragua, arguing that “there will be no link with tyrannies.”

Instead, the president-elect explained that Colombian citizens in the countries where embassies will be closed will continue to receive assistance through the concurrent representation of other diplomatic missions in the region and that the reorganization aims “to make the foreign service more efficient.”

As part of this strategy, Abelardo de la Espriella also announced the reopening of Colombia’s Embassy in Israel, which will operate in Jerusalem, a promise the new president made during the presidential campaign, and the opening of a diplomatic mission in Nigeria, to reorganize the South American country’s presence in Africa.

He also indicated that he will unify some diplomatic representations which, in his opinion, “duplicate their functions,” such as Colombia’s embassies in France and at UNESCO in Paris, as well as those in Italy and at the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) in Rome, so that a single ambassador will assume both representations.

The president-elect added that within the first 100 days of his government, he will request a technical audit of the remaining diplomatic representations in order to assess their continuity and stated that the resources saved through these measures will be used to strengthen sectors such as security, health, education, and infrastructure.

World.title: Schönbrunn Palace Orchestra Vienna to perform in Romania during Imperial Christmas Gala
World.content:
The famed Schönbrunn Palace Orchestra Vienna is set to return to Bucharest and perform at the Romanian Athenaeum on December 20 for the Imperial Christmas Gala, an event that has reached its 7th edition.

The evening's repertoire will bring together famous waltzes, lively polkas and emblematic musical pages by Johann Strauss II, alongside other jewels of Viennese classical music.

“Returning to Bucharest every December is for us a gesture of continuity and artistic affection. Imperial Christmas Gala has become a symbol of the meeting between Viennese tradition and an extraordinarily receptive and cultivated audience. It is our way of saying thank you for a year that is coming to an end,” said Peter Hosek, manager of Schönbrunn Palace Orchestra Vienna, according to Eventim.

Tickets for the event start at RON 329 (EUR 63) and can go to RON 629 (EUR 120).

Founded in 1997, Schönbrunn Palace Orchestra Vienna performs concerts at the Orangery of Schönbrunn Palace, at the Vienna State Opera and at prestigious festivals in Salzburg, being constantly invited to important stages around the world: Sweden, Finland, Germany, Italy, Romania, Japan, China and the United States.

Devoted to the Viennese tradition, the orchestra performs Johann Strauss waltzes, creations by Mozart, Haydn and Schubert, as well as works dedicated to festive moments.

In recent years, Schönbrunn Palace Orchestra Vienna has consolidated its status as an ambassador of authentic Viennese style through extensive international tours and appearances on increasingly diverse stages, from Europe to Asia and overseas. The orchestra is famous for the homogeneity of its sound, stylistic precision and stage elegance.

World.title: Mayor Acquitted of Obstructing Justice in Kosovo War Crimes Trial
World.content:
The defendants celebrate the acquittal at Pristina Basic Court, July 28, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Pristina Basic Court cleared local wartime commander Sami Lushtaku and seven others on Tuesday of obstruction of justice, witness intimidation and participation in a criminal group.

Sami Lushtaku, a commander in the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, for the region of Drenica, was accused of having from 2013 until 2015 forced two defendants to change their testimonies in the so-called Drenica case, in which Lushtaku and other KLA commanders from the Drenica region were accused of committing war crimes.

Lushtaku was not present when the judge announced the verdict, which was applauded by the public in the courtroom.

“The court could not find any convincing evidence which would prove the guilt of the defendants,” Judge Leon Perlaska said, reading the verdict. “The court assessed the testimony of the witness codenamed ‘Witness C’ where he denied that he was forced to change his statement,” Perlaska added.

Lushtaku, now mayor of the Kosovo town of Skenderaj/Srbica, was sentenced in 2015 to 12 years in prison by the Basic Court in Mitrovica for a murder committed in 1998, although the victim’s name was unknown and no body was found.

He was cleared on appeal in 2016 but his conviction for “command responsibility for allegedly violating the [bodily] integrity and health of an undefined number of civilian Albanians held at the Likovc detention centre” was upheld.

His sentence was reduced from 12 to seven years in prison by the Appeals Court. He was cleared by the Supreme Court in July 2017.

World.title: Kosovo Retrial Confirms Serbian Police Ex-Inspector’s Ten-Year Sentence
World.content:
Sacir Lutvija in court om July 28, 2026. Photo: BIRN.



Sacir Lutvija, a 65-year-old ethnic Gorani former member of the Serbian police force, was sentenced to ten years in prison in a retrial at the Pristina Basic Court, for war crimes committed during the 1998-99 war in Kosovo.

Serbian police and military forces staged a campaign of arrests of ethnic Albanian civilians and 11 of them were taken to Prizren police station in southern Kosovo, where Lutvija was among the inspectors who questioned them, according to the indictment.

Prosecutors said those arrested were beaten during the interrogation and subjected to electric shocks on their hands and genitals. One civilian died and ten others sustained serious injuries.

Lutvija, who has both Kosovo and Serbian citizenship, was arrested in October 2023 and has been in detention since then. The time in custody will be counted towards his sentence.

The Kosovo Special Prosecution charged Lutvija with unlawfully arresting and beating civilians, inhumane treatment and murder in his capacity as an inspector and police officer in Prizren. Lutvija pleaded not guilty in September last year.

Judge Kujtim Krasniqi on Tuesday ordered Lutvija to pay a court fee of 400 euros as well as 100 euros to the crime victims’ fund.

The verdict can be appealed.

Lutvija was initially sentenced to 10 years in prison by the Pristina Basic Court in November 2025.

But the Court of Appeals sent the case to a retrial in June this year having concluded that the Pristina Basic Court had not “concretely clarified the actions attributed to the accused in relation to each of the injured parties”.

The Court of Appeal also said the Basic Court failed to explained the accused’s participation in committing the crimes and “did not clarify the evidence upon which the conclusions presented in the verdict were based”.

The Gorani are a small Slavic ethnic group who mostly follow Islam and inhabit a highland triangle between Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia.

World.title: Left High and Dry: Drought Exposes Central Europe’s Water Crisis
World.content:
Water management and retention

Described as the proverbial “roof of Europe”, Czechia sees all its rivers, streams and waterways flow out of the country – a systemic and geological drainage which makes the country particularly dependent on precipitation from above.

“This is a significant disadvantage, because most of the water we manage has to be retained: in the landscape, soil, hydrogeological structures or water reservoirs,” says Adam Vizina, head of the hydrology department at the Water Management Research Institute.

Water management and retention are, therefore, key for this landlocked country, yet the authorities appear short on solutions.

“Water will always flow away, but we can reduce our vulnerability,” argues Vizina, listing measures such as slowing runoff, interconnecting water supply systems, managing water reservoirs better, or protecting the quality and quantity of groundwater.

The state reportedly spent 75 billion crowns (about 3 billion euros) in the past three years on drought adaptation, yet experts – including a report by the Supreme Audit Office published last March – have criticised the slow pace and limited scope of the measures.

The Slovak Academy of Sciences recently released its “Vision for Slovakia 2040”, an extensive 90-page framework document commissioned by the government of Robert Fico laying out the key policy challenges for the next 15 years.

Among those, the forward-looking blueprint “identifies more frequent droughts as a key consequence of climate change and argues that strengthening water management, increasing landscape water retention and improving the resilience of agriculture and ecosystems should be central priorities for Slovakia’s long-term development.”

Whether the authorities will act on the recommendations is another matter, with experts long highlighting key shortcomings in Slovakia’s water management practices, from fragmented governance between different institutions and ministries, a lack of concrete follow-through, and scattered water data hindering real-time monitoring.

Czechia and Slovakia’s subpar water-management has deep roots dating back to decades of intensive farming that followed its collectivisation in the 1950s and 1960s under Communism – with all that entailed in terms of land consolidation, water erosion and reduced soil fertility, among other environmental impacts.

On the upside, the Czech Republic continues to receive roughly the same amount of rain on average every year as it used to, according to some estimates. But the way, time and place it does are changing, as must the measures meant to retain and manage it more effectively, experts say: less rainfall in the spring but more in the fall, more intense precipitation during storms, but less frequent episodes of long-term and widespread rain.

According to Milan Vitek from the local branch of Greenpeace, Czechia might soon be faced with the choice of keeping its scarce water either in the rivers or in its fields, but won’t be able to do both. “Adaptation is something that we are decades behind when we could’ve been much further ahead,” he previously told BIRN.

Water management or retention are also recently being cited as a silver bullet to solve Hungary’s problems. Although Hungary has a renewable water reservoir of 11,833 cubic metres per person, one of the largest in Central Europe (only Slovenia and Serbia have more in the region), 95 per cent of that originates from outside and simply flows through the country.

The building of dams or hydroelectric power plants has been a politically sensitive issue since the controversial plan to build the Bos-Nagymaros dam on the Danube helped trigger popular revolt against the Communist government in 1990. Since then, proposals for new dams and hydropower projects have remained politically off-limits in Hungary.

But times are changing. Laszlo Gajdos, the new Hungarian government’s environment minister, said at the height of the extreme heat at the beginning of July that “water is one of our most valuable resources for the future”.

Gajdos said the government must do everything it can to improve water retention, even with dam construction where necessary. “We should not let water flow through Hungary; it needs to be retained somehow. Personally, I don’t like this method, but it seems inevitable building some dams,” he told RTL.hu.

The government of Peter Magyar is working on a new climate and environmental law, expected by late autumn, which is set to address water management issues.

Gajdos, who became Hungary’s first environment minister in 16 years, stressed that water retention is a regional issue requiring cooperation with neighbouring countries.

Andras Szollosi-Nagy, who used to advise international organisations including the UN on water diplomacy and is the founder member of the World Water Council, could not agree more.

“Water retention is always somehow part of national sovereignty,” Szollosi-Nagy says. “The country upstream believes all the water is theirs, but if they retain it, neighbouring countries are affected. We need integrated water management in the region.”

He says there is no silver bullet to solve all the problems: dams, reservoirs, new technologies, satellite-based monitoring and controlled flooding could all play a role.

“Hungary’s water management system has been systematically dismantled in recent decades,” he says. “Now we need to rebuild it from scratch.”

World.title: Letter from Washington: US Seeks to Score Material Goals in the Balkans
World.content:
Greetings from America, which this month celebrated 250 years of independence from the British crown under a president who has called himself a king – and is also seen that way by the many thousands of people who have joined the “No Kings” protests in the US.

Donald Trump would not even allow the kings of football, the Spanish national team who won the World Cup, to enjoy their rightful moment on the throne this month. Instead, he lingered on stage after presenting them with the trophy at the stadium in New Jersey. An awkward situation was averted by Trump’s pal, FIFA President Gianni Infantino, who pulled the US leader aside, suggesting that it was time for him to step away.

Meanwhile, beside the footballing euphoria, the US-Iran memorandum of understanding has turned out to be more of a major misunderstanding. The war has escalated, bringing new American casualties and higher fuel prices, while reopening an uncomfortable question: what is the actual endgame? If the goal is to prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons, to prevent further escalation in the Middle East, why is the United States simultaneously signing an agreement that would allow Saudi Arabia to develop the very same capability?

While all this has been happening, the Trump administration’s policy towards the Balkans has started to become increasingly clear. It is moving more aggressively into areas it considers important, such as energy, defence and infrastructure, while trying to push Russia, China and the European Union out of those spheres. Washington does not appear to be choosing its friends based on how developed their democracies are. Nor is it particularly troubled when someone in the Balkans talks about “ethnic cleansing”.

World.title: On Albania’s Adriatic Coast, Tourism Ambitions Put at Risk by Pollution
World.content:
Violeta was unimpressed by the rubbish blighting her summer holiday.

“It’s awful, isn’t it?” the 24-year-old said of the litter and construction waste strewn along beachfront at Golem Beach, a sandy stretch of Adriatic coast just south of the Albanian port city of Durres.

Golem is one of the most affordable holiday destinations in Albania, just 30 kilometres west of the capital, Tirana, and a relatively quick trip from neighbouring Kosovo. It is often packed with visitors, but Violeta said one week was enough.

“We’re going somewhere cleaner because of the pollution, like Ksamil,” she told BIRN, referring to a beach at the southern end of Albania. Pointing at rubbish, she said: “It bothers me because animals eat it and there are kids running around.”

World.title: What’s Driving the Real-Estate Price Surges in Eastern and South-East Europe?
World.content:
Rapidly rising real estate prices to the east and south of the Trieste-Szczecin line made existing dwelling owners happy - but potential buyers, especially younger people, less so.

According to Eurostat, in the first quarter of 2026, property prices in Bulgaria, Slovakia, and Croatia recorded price growth of 14 per cent over the first quarter of 2025. In a longer perspective of 3 and 10 years, the fortunes of individual countries have changed.

Generally, the total appreciation of housing real estate has been rapid, with Hungary in 10 years heading the list, followed by Bulgaria, Czechia, and Croatia.

However, Eurostat does not provide comparable data for countries southeast of Croatia, but Bosnia, Serbia, Montenegro, and others have followed similar paths. According to the Agency for Statistics of Bosnia, housing real estate prices increased by 20.4 per cent in the first quarter of 2026 compared to the first quarter of 2025. Nussubpekova recently reported a double-digit growth rate for Serbia.

World.title: North Macedonia Mourns Much-Loved Actor Goce Todorovski
World.content:
Goce Todorovski. Photo: Drama Theatre.

Actor Goce Todorovski has died aged 75, his family and the Drama Theatre in Skopje, where he spent most of his career, confirmed on Monday. The cause of death was not immediately announced.

Born in the western town of Kichevo in 1951, Todorovski graduated from the Faculty of Dramatic Arts in Skopje before joining the Drama Theatre in 1978. He went on to perform in more than 50 theatre productions, while also building a prolific career in television, radio and cinema.

His gift for comedy made him one of the country’s most enduring and popular actors.

For many Macedonians, Todorovski will be remembered above all for his appearances in the cult television series Macedonian Folk Tales (Makedonski Narodni Prikazni), whose humorous adaptations of traditional folklore became a fixture of family viewing for decades.

He was also a familiar face to generations of children through the educational television series “Scruffy Alphabet” (Bushava Azbuka), while radio audiences knew him from the long-running satirical comedy programme Hihiriku.

His film career included memorable roles in several classics of Macedonian and former Yugoslav cinema, including Happy New ’49 (Srekna Nova ’49), Weekend of the Dead (Vikend na Mrtovci), Trieste Via Skopje (Trst via Skopje), The Red Horse (Crveniot Konj), and many others.

Beyond his screen work, Todorovski was one of the leading comic actors of the Macedonian stage, collaborating with many of the country’s best-known theatre directors and helping shape the repertoire of the Drama Theatre for nearly five decades.

“Goce Todorovski never sought the audience’s affection. He won it from the moment he stepped onto the stage,” the Drama Theatre wrote in its farewell.

“His performances possessed a rare immediacy: a precise acting rhythm that seemed entirely effortless, expressive facial gestures, a distinctive stage presence, and the roguish charm with which he could effortlessly bridge the gap between the stage and the audience,” it said.

Todorovski’s performances earned numerous awards, including the state “23 October” prize for culture and the lifetime achievement award at the Vojdan Chernodrinski Theatre Festival in 2025, as well as the Presidential Order of Merit in 2023.

News of his death prompted an outpouring of tributes from fellow actors, public figures and audiences, many recalling the humour, warmth and distinctive characters that made Todorovski one of the defining faces of North Macedonia’s acting scene.

Actress Maja Andonovska Ilijevski wrote that Macedonian theatre had lost “a great man and a great actor”. Recalling their time filming the cult TV series Macedonian Folk Tales, she said Todorovski had been not only an acting legend but also a wonderful colleague, whose humour and warmth made those days unforgettable.

Andonovska said the countless characters Todorovski brought to life will remain part of the country’s collective memory, adding that “some people never truly leave – they live on through their roles, the memories of their colleagues and the love of their audience”.

Photographer Goran Anastasovski described Todorovski as “the man who made us laugh for decades” and “a giant on stage”, adding that his legacy of bringing smiles to various generations will endure.

World.title: Photos: Demolition begins at Tallinn's Eesti Näitused expo center
World.content:
Demolition has begun at Tallinn's former Eesti Näitused expo center, where a new residential development is planned along Pirita tee.

The last trade fair at the center was held in mid-June.

Mait Allas, CEO of real estate developer Metro Capital, told ERR that demolition of the Soviet-era exposition halls, which began Tuesday, is expected to take two to three months.

Metro Capital plans to begin construction of Marienberg Quarter on the nearly 7-hectare site in 2028, with plans including apartment buildings, a kindergarten, a pedestrian boulevard and green spaces.

Some nearby residents previously challenged the plans in court, but those disputes have since been resolved, and the developer says it hopes to reach agreements with neighbors going forward.

The project timeline now depends partly on approval of the site's zoning plan, which is nearing completion. Allas said he hopes it will be approved this fall, allowing design work to begin soon after.

World.title: Estonian firefighters to help put out wildfires in Italy
World.content:
Estonia's Rescue Services Agency will send firefighters to Italy to support local efforts in putting out wildfires, Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) has said.

France, Spain, northern Portugal, and northern Italy have been hit hardest by the current wildfires in Southern Europe.

Tsahkna said that the Estonian Rescue Services Agency wildfire firefighting team will join local response efforts in Sardinia, Italy, to fight the fires.

"We are deeply grateful to every firefighter and emergency responder risking so much to protect lives, homes and nature," he said in a statement on social media.

"These devastating wildfires remind us that strengthening our resilience, caring for our environment and preparing for a changing climate is ultimately about protecting people, their homes and the places they cherish," he added.

My heart goes out to everyone affected by the devastating wildfires across Southern Europe.

World.title: Prosecutor's Office puts money from conditionally terminated cases into a lottery pool
World.content:
Financial obligations imposed in Estonian criminal cases ended through conditional termination used to have to be paid into the state treasury, but now that money may, through a lottery, end up with NGOs. Last week, two local sports clubs became €6000 richer.

Previously, in cases ended with conditional termination, the Prosecutor's Office could direct the person entering into the agreement to perform community service or require them to pay a set amount into state revenues.

The Prosecutor's Office suspected MP Tõnis Mölder of accepting a bribe and attempted to have his parliamentary immunity removed. Although the Riigikogu did not vote in favor of that, proceedings continued with the two alleged bribe givers and the intermediary.

Last week it emerged that the cases of those two individuals ended with conditional termination, and both men had to pay €6000 for that purpose. However, the money did not go to the state treasury but instead to two sports clubs — the Järvamaa Sports Association and Sakala Biathlon.

Kristjan Lill Autor/allikas: ERR/Vikerraadio

Kristjan Lill, senior prosecutor at the Northern District Prosecutor's Office, said in an interview that since 2024 it has been possible to direct the financial obligation imposed under conditional termination to targeted use in the public interest.

According to Lill, the recipients may be non‑profit organizations, foundations, and religious associations that are listed by the Tax and Customs Board (EMTA) as eligible for income‑tax benefits. The prosecutor must propose such a "donation."

When making the selection, the prosecutor can narrow the possible choices based on several criteria, with the final selection determined by lottery.

"Whether to choose organizations operating across Estonia or, from the perspective of the Viru District Prosecutor's Office, perhaps organizations in Ida‑Virumaa and Lääne‑Virumaa," Lill said, adding that the selection can also be made by field of activity. For example, the list includes culture, children, animals, and sports, as well as a separate category for supporting Ukraine.

Lill said NGOs and foundations should not expect money to start flowing toward them.

"It's more like a lottery, and certainly not everyone will get money. In the EMTA's list — I may be mistaken — there are between 1000 and 2000 organizations."

As an interesting detail, Lill pointed out that if a suspect or accused person accepts such an obligation and pays the amount accordingly, they can deduct the donation as tax‑exempt income up to €8400.

World.title: Estonian schools struggle to fill math and primary‑class teaching jobs
World.content:
Schools are looking most actively — through public job postings — for mathematics teachers and primary‑class teachers, but English teachers are also in very high demand. The largest number of vacancies is in Tallinn and Harju County, but teachers are frequently missing in Lääne‑Virumaa and Tartu County as well.

In the Õpetajate Leht job listings, schools are seeking 147 education workers — 134 teachers and 13 special‑education or support staff.

There are 92 active postings in total. Although some advertised positions may already be filled, the data provides a good overview of which types of teachers are most needed in which municipalities.

Olga Selištševa, director of Tallinn Tõnismäe State High School, which is looking for four teachers, said the high demand is nothing new. "It was the same last year and the year before. It's an annual situation," she said.

According to Selištševa, the large number of people aspiring to become teachers may give the impression that many new teachers are entering schools, but in reality most who enroll in teacher‑training programs are already working in schools and simply want to obtain the qualification.

"New people aren't coming, and that's the problem," she said.

Tallinn Avatud Kool opened on September 1 in Tallinn, one of two new schools opening in the capital this year. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

By county, Harju County has the most vacancies, with 32 job postings. Lääne‑Virumaa is looking for 12 education workers, and Tartu County for 10.

Pärnu County and Järva County each have five openings, Ida‑Virumaa four, and Jõgeva, Põlva, and Valga counties three each. Rapla, Viljandi, and Võru counties each have two, and Lääne County has one vacancy.

By position type, the largest number of postings are for primary‑class teachers, with 34 vacancies. Among subject teachers, mathematics teachers are most sought after, with 26 postings.

Schools are looking for 19 English teachers and 15 music teachers. There are 11 postings for Estonian language and literature teachers, and four for Estonian language teachers.

Physics teachers are needed for eight positions and chemistry teachers for four, plus one combined physics‑or‑chemistry posting.

Among support specialists and positions related to teaching students with special needs, the most vacancies are for speech therapists, who are sought by 19 institutions.

In many cases, schools need more than one new teacher.

World.title: Infrastructure in Estonia surges while apartment construction falters
World.content:
Apartment building in Estonia is currently sluggish, while infrastructure is booming, says Tarmo Pohlak, board member of the construction company Nordecon.

Pohlak says that the many construction cranes currently visible in central Tallinn represent only the tip of the iceberg, and the decisions to build those buildings were often made long ago.

At the same time, major infrastructure projects are underway in Estonia: 45 kilometers of 2+2 road are being built on the Tallinn–Pärnu highway, and part of the Tallinn–Tartu highway is also out to tender.

Construction of Rail Baltic is ongoing as well, though it is not very visible to ordinary people in the cityscape. Based on current knowledge, Estonia will complete its entire section up to Ikla on the Latvian border, and the pace will be very fast until 2030. "There are very large volumes of concrete, earthworks and other materials," Pohlak said.

According to him, Nordecon is also building several national defense facilities deep in the forests, where the work volumes are quite large.

Pohlak says the economy is currently highly volatile, yet construction companies are required to adhere to fixed prices. "Someone made the comparison that if Eesti Pank says it cannot produce very precise forecasts, then construction companies, when submitting bids, must be able to foresee everything and factor it into their price."

"Reedene intervjuu": Tarmo Pohlak Autor/allikas: Ken Mürk/ERR

In the private sector, Nordecon is currently building two hotels — one in Viljandi and the other on the shore of Lake Peipus. "Both entrepreneurs have taken a big risk, and we are happy to build."

But when it comes to apartment construction, current volumes are incomparably smaller than before the COVID pandemic.

Developing commercial real estate is also difficult at the moment. "You have to believe you will have clients, or in the case of an office building, you must know who you are building it for. You have to secure an anchor tenant. Entrepreneur Urmas Sõõrumaa signed a contract with SEB Bank, which is a very large anchor, and thanks to that the major Talsinki Quarter project went ahead. It is a very large private investment in central Tallinn, but without the SEB contract, that plot would be silent today," Pohlak noted.

The new 'Talsinki' retail and residential area in central Tallinn. Source: Talsinki arhitektuuri loovad arhitektuuribürood Arhitekt 11 ja HGA, maastikuarhitektuuri autor on TajuRuum. Sisearhitektuuri kujundavad studio ARGUS (kodud) ja LÄVI (bürood). Ehitab Bildgren Ehitus.

The state is improving infrastructure, but practically no new large state building projects are coming, Pohlak said. The only known project is the Siuru Cultural Center in Tartu. There are some schools and kindergartens, but from the builder's perspective these are relatively small.

Pohlak recalled that in spring 2022, at the start of the war in Ukraine, a materials shortage emerged reminiscent of Soviet times. "I was on the client side then, walking around the site. One wall was insulated with one type of mineral wool, another with a different type, and a third with a third type. If you asked the main contractor why, they used whatever they could get at that moment. If nothing was available, work stopped. The price of rebar doubled or tripled overnight."

According to Pohlak, the building sector adapted to the situation, but now there are new problems. The situation in the Strait of Hormuz pushes oil and gas prices up and down. Many construction materials — and transport — are tied to oil and gas prices.

Pohlak noted that if all Ukrainian construction workers were to leave Estonia, the impact would be catastrophic. "Without foreign labor it would be very difficult, because there are not enough workers. And they are very capable."

Cranes building the Rail Baltica terminal in Tallinn. Source: Mait Ots/ERR

World.title: Ida-Viru County seeks tourism rebrand beyond Soviet-era 'ghost town' image
World.content:
Being adjacent to the eastern border and its distance from Tallinn mean Ida-Viru County has long been somewhat off the beaten track, attracting more niche types of tourism than other parts of the country.

One classic example of this is the former mining town of Viivikonna, famed for being a ghost town, though there are people living there again nowadays.

Local residents are often keen to move away from the old Soviet tag and embrace something new.

"We want to turn [Viivikonna] back into a holiday destination, with beautiful backyards. Perhaps in the future it could become an example of how to turn an ugly town into a beautiful settlement," Priit Orav, who has worked as a tour guide in the area for around 25 years, suggested.

Viivikonna as it is now has, thanks to its abandoned and eerie nature, long been a popular destination for visitors, tourists, and even filmmakers exploring new locations.

Ruined building in Viivikonna. Source: Chris Feichtner/Flickr

"I think there is already enough material about it on YouTube, and filmmakers from all over the world have been there. Now I think it is time to draw a line under it. We need to move on from this Soviet nostalgia. Right next door, beautiful private homes have been built or old ones have been renovated, and everything is already beginning to take on a European appearance," Orav explained, talking to "Vikerhommik".

The transformation process is already underway, and the larger buildings have largely been demolished, leaving only the former schoolhouse and a few smaller residential buildings.

These latter buildings are often being used as homes nowadays in any case, Orav noted. "What is left are smaller houses that were once built for four families. They have become homes for one or two families, with beautiful gardens. People do care about their surroundings."

In the quarter of a century Orav has worked as a guide in Viivikonna, he has conducted around 100 tours of the so-called ghost town, and so has seen the transformation at first hand. "I have seen this change and I have also seen the reaction of the local residents. They have for a long time been tired of the fact that so many people go there, and that the place has attracted the attention of social media around the world," he said.

The same can be said of the surrounding area. "I hope this place will develop into a quiet, nice settlement with low-density housing. Just 10 kilometers away is Sillamäe, which has also become very beautiful nowadays," Orav added.

The center of Sillamäe is an example of typical Stalinist architecture. Source: Visit Estonia/ Tauri Taal.

He also often conducts tours of Sillamäe, a nearby port town with notable neoclassical architecture dating mostly to the Stalinist era. "Of course, it has a Russian or Soviet 'accent', but that is exactly what people come to see, because there is no other city like it in Estonia. Now we just have to wait for the local residents of Sillamäe to grasp that the old town of Sillamäe is an attraction, and that the buildings and exterior façades ultimately need to be restored."

Other highlights include the beach at Narva-Jõesuu, downstream from Narva and a resort town. It is very difficult to find anything similar to Narva-Jõesuu elsewhere, Orav said, also bringing out the Aidu quarry, where a versatile water sports center has been established, as characterizing a new emerging trend.

"The Kiviõli ash hills have found their place, but the new rowing channel at Aidu and everything else around it, as well as the underground mine in Kohtla-Nõmme, are things that only we have; there is nothing like them elsewhere in Estonia."

Kiviõli hosts a notable motocross circuit, skiing can be done on some of the artificial slopes left over from mine tailings, and the forests of Ida-Viru County are home to a population of Siberian Flying Squirrels.

Ultimately what makes Ida-Viru County a special tourism destination is its natural beauty: Its vast array of rivers, lakes, the sea, forests, bogs, and wetlands, Orav concluded.

World.title: New ambassador to the US: I'm ready to run in presidential elections
World.content:
Incoming Estonian ambassador to the United States Hannes Hanso has said he would be willing to be a candidate at September's Estonian presidential elections, if asked.

Hanso, 54, until recently Estonia's ambassador to China, said he would make a good president if elected, adding more than one party has floated the idea.

"It is true that two or three parties have discussed my possible candidacy in various formats. Also in a broader circle. That is, in itself, a great honor for me," the newly appointed representative to Washington, told Vikerraadio's Uudis+ program Tuesday.

In response to the host's question about what his response would be if party leaders asked him to run for president, Hanso said: "What would I say? It would be tough for us to reorganize our family life once again, but I would definitely be ready. I have no doubt that I would be a good president of the republic."

Hanso noted his resume includes a stint as minister of defense (2015-2016). He has also served in local government, including as a mayor, and on local councils as well, and national politics as a past Riigikogu member, where he chaired the Riigikogu's foreign affairs and national defense committees at various times. He was also briefly an MEP (2019).

"If those are the experiences and competencies that are being sought, then as a citizen it would almost be irresponsible to say 'no,' if such a consensus could be built around me. To refuse to take on that responsibility. Then we would have to reshuffle our cards once again, and the children would also be very happy that they could finally live in Estonia again. In short, Hannes Hanso would not throw in the towel and would say 'yes'."

Hanso also said he does not like the situation which has emerged around Estonia's presidential election process and the upcoming election in particular.

Ballots being counted at the first round of the 2021 presidential election. Source: Erik Peinar, Chancellery of the Riigikogu

"The world is unstable and turbulent. We need some clarity, and people should be honest. If they have an ambition to become president, they should say so. Be a man and say it, or be a woman and say it: 'Yes, I am interested. I believe we all have a responsibility for these matters.' Standing behind a bush, hedging, or keeping the door open without saying anything – there is really no need for such fear. It is the greatest honor a person can have: to be the head of state, the country's leader."

Hanso was appointed Estonia's next ambassador to the U.S. in early June, replacing Kristjan Prikk, who is to become Estonia's ambassador to NATO later in the year. Hanso had been ambassador to Beijing up to his new appointment.

Hanso's declaration comes at a time when several other public figures have either been put forward by politicians as candidates, or declared their own interest in running. The first group includes Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise, while former Defense League commander Riho Ühtegi is in the latter camp.

Estonia's presidents are elected by the Riigikogu in the first instance, with a majority of 68 at the 101-seat chamber needed, meaning cross-party support of coalition and opposition parties is required for a candidate to get voted in.

If three rounds of voting draw a blank, the process moves to the regional electoral college.

Nominations open for candidates on August 21, and close August 24. The Riigikogu voting rounds start on September 2.

Hanso was a member of the Social Democratic Party (SDE) from February 2009 until June 2019.

World.title: Hiiumaa and Saaremaa residents can soon travel with discounted tickets
World.content:
The Ministry of Regional Affairs has revoked time-limited changes for discounted ferry tickets for Saaremaa and Hiiumaa following strong criticism.

Under the initial proposal, residents of Saaremaa and Hiiumaa would have had to wait 36 ​​hours after a disruption to the direct ferry link between the two islands before they could take a detour through the mainland using a discounted ticket.

The plan met with strong opposition from island residents.

Minister of Regional Affairs and Agriculture Hendrik Johannes Terras (Eesti 200) explained that a new system is set to take effect this autumn, allowing permanent residents of Saaremaa and Hiiumaa to travel from the mainland to the neighboring island at a discounted rate year-round.

"The mechanism will be the same as the one currently used, where the discount applies to the passenger and the vehicle under the same conditions. Eligibility is based on official residency registration in either municipality," Terras added.

World.title: Iraq’s oil exports hit 526,000 bpd in May and June
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s average oil exports in May and June 2026 were roughly 526,470 barrels per day, compared to about 329,500 barrels per day in April, amid ongoing shipping and energy disruptions in the Gulf region.

The revenues generated from Iraqi oil exports saw an improvement over the last two months, supported by a relative increase in shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and the activation of alternative export routes.

Oil prices fluctuated, remaining high at around $100 per barrel during May before falling below that level in June.

The rising oil prices boosted Iraq’s export income in May and June 2026, when there were fears about supply constraints and increased Asian demand, notably from China and India.

Iraqi oil exports have been under growing strain since the beginning of March, following the suspension of loading operations at southern ports due to the US war against Iran, which had a direct impact on marine security in the Strait of Hormuz.

According to the State Organization for Marketing of Oil (SOMO), Iraq’s total oil exports in May and June 2026 were roughly 32.11 million barrels, with a monthly average of over 16 million barrels.

The country’s oil exports reached 9.88 million barrels in April and around 18.6 million barrels in March.

Iraqi oil export earnings in May and June 2026 reached approximately $2.33 billion, averaging $1.16 billion per month, compared to $1.87 billion in April, $1.95 billion in March, and approximately $6.81 billion in February.

Experts believe that the current price levels of oil are likely to provide Baghdad with a better financial margin to mitigate some losses incurred from the significant decline in exports, even amidst ongoing security tensions in the region.

World.title: Iraqi PM arrives in Turkey on an official visit
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi arrived in the Turkish capital, Ankara, on Tuesday, for an official visit following an invitation from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Al-Zaidi said in a statement on X that his trip to Turkey will focus on investments, water, and development projects, as well as efforts to enhance stability in the region.

Turkish media highlighted the significance of the visit, as it is expected to broaden constructive collaboration between the two countries, particularly in the areas of water, energy, security, and economic cooperation, according to the state-run news agency (INA).

In addition to trade, security cooperation, and combating terrorism, al-Zaidi will discuss establishing a cooperative water management entity based on shared interests, as well as scientific collaboration and investment in advanced technology, to serve the interests of both Iraq and Turkey.

Al-Zaidi is scheduled to fly to Saudi Arabia on Thursday for an official visit, following his diplomatic trip to the Turkish capital, Ankara.

The trip is part of a larger regional diplomatic tour aiming to maintain regional balance and strengthen Iraq’s business connections.

The prime minister recently conducted high-level diplomatic visits to the United States on July 13 and Iran on July 23.

World.title: Ukraine rejects Iraqi official’s claims of Ukrainian cell operating in Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Tuesday dismissed statements by Iraq’s National Security Adviser Qasim Al-Aboudi, who claimed that Iraqi authorities had arrested a Ukrainian-linked cell responsible for carrying out attacks inside the country.

In an official statement, the ministry said the allegations were “groundless” and noted that no evidence had been presented to support the claims. It also pointed out that Al-Aboudi himself acknowledged during a televised interview that investigations into the matter were still ongoing.

According to the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry, Iraqi authorities did not communicate any information or concerns through diplomatic channels before the allegations were made publicly.

The ministry said that if Iraqi officials possessed credible evidence, the issue should have been raised through official diplomatic mechanisms rather than announced during a television interview. Instead, Kyiv said it first learned of the accusations through media reports.

Furthermore, Ukraine described the public remarks by a senior Iraqi official as “unacceptable and irresponsible” in the absence of supporting evidence. The ministry stressed that such statements contradict the principles of mutual respect between friendly nations and risk undermining relations between Iraq and Ukraine.

At the same time, Kyiv reaffirmed that it considers Iraq an important partner in the Middle East and remains committed to strengthening political, economic, and humanitarian cooperation between the two countries.

The Foreign Ministry also argued that the allegations mirror Russian propaganda narratives aimed at damaging Ukraine’s international reputation and weakening its partnerships across the Middle East.

Additionally, the statement suggested that the incident could have resulted from external information influence or formed part of a coordinated information campaign intended to disrupt Iraqi-Ukrainian relations.

Ukraine called on Iraqi authorities to address what it described as unfounded allegations and to prevent state institutions from promoting misinformation that could serve the interests of third parties.

The Ukrainian response follows remarks made on Monday by National Security Adviser Qasim Al-Aboudi during an interview on Dijlah TV. Al-Aboudi said Iraqi intelligence had identified what he described as Ukrainian interference inside Iraq and claimed security forces had arrested several individuals who allegedly carried out attacks on Iraqi territory.

He further stated that those detained confessed during questioning to working on behalf of Ukraine. However, Al-Aboudi did not identify the facilities allegedly targeted or specify whether the alleged operations extended beyond Iraq’s borders.

He also acknowledged that investigations into attacks carried out inside Iraq remain complex and require further examination before responsibility can be definitively assigned.

World.title: Iraqi PM expands powers as political deadlock delays cabinet completion
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – A dispute over Iraq’s remaining vacant cabinet positions has expanded beyond the selection of ministers, with political factions now focusing on the growing authority of the Office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, according to a report published by Al-Mada newspaper.

The debate follows the leak of an official document indicating that Prime Minister Ali Falih Al-Zaidi has reactivated and expanded the powers of the Commander-in-Chief Office, placing several key security institutions under its supervision while the Ministries of Interior and Defense remain without permanent ministers.

According to Al-Mada, several political sources believe the expanded office significantly increases the prime minister’s direct oversight of Iraq’s security apparatus.

The report says the office now oversees the Ministries of Interior and Defense, the Counter-Terrorism Service, the National Intelligence Service, the National Security Service, the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), border crossings, military industries, and other security-related institutions.

Consequently, some political figures have described the move as a “quiet coup” against Iraq’s post-2003 political framework, arguing that it centralizes authority within the prime minister’s office while reducing the practical influence of future ministers.

Meanwhile, Iraq’s cabinet remains incomplete, with only 14 ministries currently filled while nine ministerial portfolios remain vacant. According to the report, political negotiations have become increasingly complicated, as disagreements now extend beyond candidate names to broader questions of political influence and institutional control.

Sources cited by Al-Mada said the State of Law Coalition has proposed rotating senior security positions as part of efforts to break the deadlock, particularly regarding the Interior Ministry, which traditionally falls under the Shiite political share, while the Defense Ministry is typically allocated to Sunni representatives.

However, negotiations have yet to produce a breakthrough.

At the same time, Al-Mada reported that U.S. objections have become one of the main obstacles preventing completion of the cabinet. Political sources quoted in the report claim Washington opposes appointing individuals affiliated with armed factions to ministerial positions or senior executive offices.

The report says these objections have complicated negotiations among members of the Coordination Framework, with some factions insisting that if their nominees are rejected, similar restrictions should apply to other political parties. As a result, discussions over the remaining cabinet positions have largely stalled.

Political analysts interviewed by Al-Mada argue that the continued delay in appointing ministers has allowed Prime Minister Al-Zaidi greater flexibility in managing state institutions through acting officials and appointments within his office.

According to the report, some political parties fear that prolonging the vacancies could further strengthen the prime minister’s influence over Iraq’s security establishment, making future ministerial appointments less significant.

The report also notes that recent anti-corruption campaigns and shifting political alliances have altered the balance of power within the Coordination Framework, adding another layer of complexity to negotiations.

Supporters of the government, however, argue that the current arrangements are necessary to maintain continuity while negotiations continue.

Officials quoted by Al-Mada said acting appointments and the reactivation of the Commander-in-Chief Office ensure that security institutions continue functioning despite the absence of permanent ministers.

They also expressed confidence that political forces will eventually reach an agreement to complete the cabinet, stressing that Iraq faces significant challenges, including anti-corruption efforts, security reforms, weapons control, and economic pressures linked to oil exports.

Nevertheless, the report suggests that political parties continue to use the vacant ministries as leverage in negotiations with the prime minister, making the timeline for completing the government uncertain.

World.title: US drone shot down in western Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – An unknown drone, first claimed by Iranian official media IRIB as a US surveillance one, crashed within a residential complex near the Haditha Dam in the western Iraqi province of Anbar.

Iraqi police and security agencies later indicated that the drone’s origin remains unknown, according to Al-Jazeera.

The debris was discovered blazing in a residential compound near the Haditha Dam in Anbar.

Local police stated that there were no recorded injuries or civilian deaths as a result of the collision.

Iranian state media swiftly released images of the smoking debris, claiming it was a US drone shot down amid broader regional activity.

The incident took place during a night of broad military conflict in Iraq, which included many drone attacks and defensive responses.

At least four Iranian drones attacked targets northeast of the capital of Iraqi Kurdistan, Erbil, sparking a huge defensive reaction, including over ten US jets and drones sent to inspect the skies.

Air defense systems were activated at Anbar’s Ain al-Asad Air Base in response to a drone strike.

Explosions, alleged suicide drones, and radar interruptions were also reported at Camp Taji, Balad Air Base, and Imam Ali Base in southern Iraq.

The US military has not publicly verified the loss of any aircraft in Anbar. Investigations into the model and operator of the crashed drone are still underway.

World.title: Al Zaidi: Iraq and Turkey can build a regional success story through economic integration
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi said on Tuesday that the Middle East needs new success stories built on economic integration rather than conflict, arguing that Iraq and Turkey have the potential to create a model regional partnership through joint investment, infrastructure, and trade.

The remarks came in an article published by Turkey’s Anadolu Agency ahead of Al Zaidi’s official visit to Ankara, where he is expected to meet Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and senior officials.

Al Zaidi said relations between Iraq and Turkey have traditionally focused on managing issues such as security, water resources, trade, and border crossings. However, he argued that regional changes require a more ambitious vision centered on economic cooperation.

He said Iraq has chosen a path of stability, reform, and development, prioritizing a stronger economy, an effective state, and balanced foreign relations that make regional cooperation a pillar of growth.

According to Al Zaidi, Turkey’s industrial base, strategic location, and expertise in infrastructure, energy, and transportation complement Iraq’s geographic position, creating an opportunity to establish one of the region’s most significant economic partnerships.

The prime minister highlighted the Development Road Project, describing it as more than an Iraqi initiative. He said the corridor could redefine economic connectivity in the Middle East by linking Gulf ports with Asian and European markets.

He added that the project would not only reduce shipping times but also create new cities, industrial zones, investment opportunities, and thousands of jobs, while establishing a new economic artery connecting ports to global markets.

Al Zaidi also stressed that security cooperation remains essential, saying Iraq’s and Turkey’s security are closely linked and require mutual respect for sovereignty as well as joint efforts to combat terrorism and organized crime.

On water issues, he said water is no longer simply a technical matter but a development challenge affecting millions of people. He called for a shared approach based on mutual interests, scientific cooperation, and investment in modern technologies to strengthen water and food security.

“The Middle East needs new success stories,” Al Zaidi wrote, adding that Iraq and Turkey can provide one if they move beyond traditional cooperation toward genuine economic integration.

He said every joint investment, factory, transport route, and energy project represents an investment in regional stability, arguing that lasting stability is built through shared projects rather than conflict.

Later on Tuesday, Al Zaidi departed for Ankara at the head of a high-level government delegation. According to the Prime Minister’s Office, the visit will focus on strengthening bilateral cooperation in the fields of economy, water, security, investment, and regional affairs.

The two sides are also expected to review the implementation of existing agreements and memoranda of understanding, while discussing progress on joint infrastructure projects, including the Development Road initiative.

World.title: Drone attack targets Khor Mor gas field in northern Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Drone attacks targeted the Khor Mor gas field in the northern Iraqi province of Sulaymaniyah in the early hours of Tuesday.

The attack on the field, which is Iraq’s largest gas field with reserves estimated at 8.2 trillion cubic feet, was part of a coordinated wave of suspected Iranian drone attacks against the Kurdistan region of Iraq.

Iranian official media reported an attack on the gas field, which is operated by the UAE-based Pearl Consortium that includes Dana Gas and Crescent Petroleum.

The gas field supplies the majority of the electricity in Iraqi Kurdistan.

According to reports, the strikes were carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which targets Iranian Kurdish resistance groups and US interests in the region.

A few days ago, Iraqi Kurdistan’s Prime Minister Masoud Barzani stated that repeated security threats and drone attacks had caused energy companies to cut domestic output, seriously affecting the region’s electrical infrastructure.

The escalation takes place amid significant geopolitical challenges. On Monday, US President Donald Trump said he was ready to resume military action against Iran if diplomatic efforts to reach a nuclear deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz failed.

Trump stated that he has temporarily stopped military strikes against Iran to give negotiations a chance to work.

World.title: Iraq, Australia cooperate to sentence alleged drug trafficker to life imprisonment
World.content:
An Iraqi court has sentenced convicted drug trafficker Kazem Hamad to life imprisonment after finding him guilty of drug trafficking and links to transnational organized crime, in a case that involved close cooperation between Iraqi and Australian authorities.

The ruling marks a significant development in Iraq’s ongoing campaign against organized crime and narcotics trafficking.

In a statement issued on Monday, Iraq’s judiciary described Hamad as “one of the most wanted individuals by Iraqi and international courts.” According to the judiciary, Hamad was responsible for smuggling large quantities of heroin into both Iraq and Australia.

The statement also accused him of involvement with transnational criminal networks engaged in drug trafficking, money laundering, murder, kidnapping, extortion, and organized violence.

Australian authorities have identified Hamad as a key figure in Melbourne’s so-called “tobacco wars,” a violent conflict between organized crime groups competing for control of the illicit tobacco and vape market.

The turf war has been linked to more than 200 arson attacks, firebombings, and extortion incidents across the Australian city. Hamad was deported from Australia in 2023 and was arrested in Iraq in January 2026, where prosecutors charged him with smuggling narcotics into both countries.

The Australian Federal Police (AFP) confirmed earlier this year that it had provided operational information to support Iraq’s investigation. AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett said in February that the agency would continue cooperating with Iraqi authorities while pursuing its own investigation into Hamad and his alleged criminal network under Operation Carmen.

Australian investigators have also linked Hamad to several serious crimes, including allegations that he played a role in the December 2024 firebombing of Melbourne’s Adass Israel Synagogue, according to Australian media reports.

The life sentence comes as Iraq continues to intensify its fight against drug trafficking and organized crime. Despite imposing some of the region’s toughest penalties, including life imprisonment and the death penalty for major narcotics offenses, Iraq has experienced a sharp rise in drug trafficking and addiction since 2003.

Officials say authorities have arrested thousands of suspects in recent years as part of nationwide anti-drug operations. Iraq was recently ranked third globally in combating narcotics at the World Police Summit in the United Arab Emirates, reflecting the country’s expanding efforts to dismantle trafficking networks.

World.title: Don't damage water bodies under garb of beautification: SC warns Bihar government
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Taking a stern view of allegations that the Bihar government is filling parts of three historic ponds in Darbhanga to create public amenities such as recreation spaces and stalls, the Supreme Court on Tuesday warned the state govt ânot to touch the water bodies under the garb of beautificationâ without its approval.

A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta directed the state govt to immediately stall the ongoing work related to the âBeautification and Rejuvenation of Gangasagar, Digghi and Harahi Lakeâ project. Although the state refuted the allegations of encroachment and urged the court to allow the work to continue, describing it as an ambitious project worth more than â¹100 crore, the bench refused to budge and ordered that no further work be carried out.

âYou cannot fill up water bodies under the garb of beautification. Do not touch the water ponds, keep your hands off and tell your officers not to touch the ponds,â the bench told advocate Manish Kumar, who was appearing for the state government.

TOI had reported on July 13, with photographs, that three ponds in Darbhanga were being filled with soil and boulders to make way for stalls and footpaths, despite strong opposition from local residents and environmentalists.





TOI report on Darbhanga ponds

Advocate Renu Prajapati, appearing for the Darbhanga-based voluntary group Talab Bachao Abhiyan (TBA), informed the bench that the three ponds form part of a list of protected wetlands and that any construction on their banks would violate rules and earlier rulings of the apex court. She also pointed out that the state, in its own affidavit, had admitted that around four acres of the ponds would be filled under the project.

In its affidavit, the state claimed that no arbitrary filling of the water bodies was taking place and that the activity was highly restricted and meticulously planned âEarth Filling & Stone Pitchingâ work.

âThis process is a necessity to stabilise and strengthen the severely eroded embankments, directly executing the mandate of the NGTâs order. Furthermore, the soil-filling footprint is strictly limited â for instance, constituting exactly 1.00 acre out of the 37.73-acre Harahi site, 1.42 acres out of the 50.97 acres at Digghi Lake, and 1.69 acres out of 44.22 acres at Gangasagar Lake,â the affidavit stated.

After a brief hearing, the bench directed the government to stop the work and ensure that the area of the ponds remain intact and is not reduced by filling..

Justifying the project, the state said the integration of public amenities is aimed at managing footfall, ensuring public hygiene, and preventing future degradation.

The court was hearing a plea filed by retired academicians, environmentalists and concerned citizens under the banner of TBA.

They are seeking urgent intervention to halt the filling of three historic ponds in Darbhanga â all 800â900 years old and integral to the cityâs identity.

âSince the State is acting in contravention of these orders and having been left with no other remedy, the petitioner herein is constrained to approach this court seeking an urgent and immediate remedy to stop further filling of the ponds and further to remove all the encroachments in and around the three ponds of Darbhanga and restore those to their original position as depicted in the maps of the years 1868 and 1960,â the petition stated.

In its response, the state submitted: âIt is respectfully submitted that in order to tackle the unregulated access which historically led to the lakes becoming open garbage dumps, the project provides structured and safe public utility interfaces including the construction of 11 designated bathing ghats equipped with 5 changing rooms and 7 sanitary toilet blocks to eliminate open defecation and water contamination.

â

World.title: As Maldives president seeks SAARC summit, India says cooperation requires goodwill
World.content:
Maldives President Mohamed Muizzu

With Maldives President Mohamed Muizzu calling for resumption of the biennial SAARC summit process, India reiterated Tuesday that it's Pakistan's support for cross-border terrorism that has blocked the intergovernmental organisation, which was conceived to build a connected and integrated South Asia. Muizzu in his Independence Day speech had also offered to act as a mediator between India and Pakistan to advance talks for an early leaders' summit.The last SAARC summit was held in 2014 in Nepal. The next summit that Pakistan was scheduled to host in 2016 could never take place as India pulled out because of the cross-border Uri terrorist attack. India has since maintained that regional cooperation under SAARC is adversely affected due to continued support to cross-border terrorism and interference in the internal affairs of member-states by Pakistan.Member-states like the Maldives, Bangladesh and Nepal have from time-to-time sought revival of the summit. "India favors strong regional cooperation and has been working towards it for several decades. Everyone in South Asia is aware of which country and what activities are responsible for stymieing SAARC," said MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, adding that cooperation requires goodwill.The official was responding to a question about Muizzu's remarks in which he had sought "reactivation' of SAARC calling it vital for regional peace and security."We must bring matters to the point where the leaders of SAARC resume holding summits once again," said Muizzu."To those parties among whom differences have arisen in this regard, the Maldives calls upon you to set those matters aside, to prioritise friendship for the sake of regional development and regional peace, and to come to the negotiating table. Should the task prove challenging, the Maldives stands ready to take the initiative and act as a mediator to advance those discussions," said the president, adding that SAARC must be operationalised once again and that his administration would always champion peace.Muizzu also said that SAARC had brought numerous benefits to the region"However, we now witness a span of some nine years during which this organisation has been rendered, or has become, dysfunctional. Given that the foreign policy of the Maldives is structured...upon the principle that differences should be addressed through consultation, by bringing concerns to the discussion table, reaching resolutions, and moving forward in a manner that benefits all, the reactivation of SAARC is equally vital for regional peace and security," he added.Muizzu said his government's foreign policy was based on the conviction that if differences are left to be settled by violence and force, no resolution will ever be found.

World.title: Demand for MSP, reforms: Protesting farmers breach police barricades enroute to Bhopal
World.content:
Farmers march from Narmadapuram to Bhopal (ANI image)

Farmers marching from Narmadapuram to Bhopal demanding 100 per cent procurement of moong at the Minimum Support Price (MSP) breached police barricades on Tuesday as they entered the Madhya Pradesh capital, intensifying their protest against the state government.Visuals from Bhopal showed farmers crossing police barricades while carrying the Tricolour. Police did not use force and eventually opened the route, allowing the farmers to proceed into the city.The protest, organised under the banner of the Samyukta Kisan Morcha, began on Monday with a sit-in at Sethanighat in Narmadapuram, where farmers recited the Hanuman Chalisa before starting their march towards Bhopal, PTI reported.Earlier, police had attempted to stop the march by erecting barricades at Bhopal Tiraha and other locations. District Magistrate Somesh Mishra and Superintendent of Police Saikrishna S. Thota held talks with the protesting farmers on National Highway-69, but the discussions failed to break the deadlock.The farmers are demanding 100 per cent procurement of moong under MSP, a solution to issues related to the e-token system, and the timely availability of fertilisers at reasonable prices.

World.title: 'Clock it', 'delulu': How Gen Z lingo took over Parliament during anti-paper leak Bill debate
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Lok Sabha debate on the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026 on Tuesday wasn't just about examination reforms and paper leaks. It also turned into an unexpected showcase of Gen Z vocabulary, with MPs across party lines dropping terms such as "clock it", "MIA", "FOMO" and "delulu" to sharpen their political arguments.

From the treasury benches praising the Centre's reforms to the opposition attacking the government's handling of the NEET controversy, lawmakers reached for internet slang more commonly found on social media than in Parliament.

'Clock it'

BJP MP Bansuri Swaraj used the Gen Z phrase "clock it" â a slang term used to recognise something â while backing the proposed legislation.

Speaking in favour of the Bill, she said, "Borrowing Gen Z's language, I would have to say that Modiji clocked it at providing this legislative solution."

Calling the amendment a "transformative" step, Swaraj argued that it reflected the government's commitment to protecting the integrity of public examinations.

"I am standing in support of the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026. This is a transformative amendment. Its necessity is not only evident, but it is also the demand of the present time. Bringing this amendment is proof of the sensitivity of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his committed government.





Speaker Sir, when a competitive examination is compromised, its impact is not limited to the candidate whose future is put at stake," she added.

NDA MP's 'delulu' jibe at opposition

Shiv Sena MP Shrikant Lata Eknath Shinde turned to multiple Gen Z expressions to mock the opposition's protests over the NEET paper leak.

"I'd like to sum up the opposition's protest in Gen Z language. They were MIA (missing in action) for the first 37 days and did not go to Jantar Mantar.

Then came FOMO (fear of missing out), so they held a protest outside the Prime Minister's residence. Finally, they became 'delulu' (delusional), believing the protesting students would join themâbut no one did," Shinde said.

Priyanka's swipe at PM's videos

Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, meanwhile, invoked Gen Z while targeting Prime Minister Narendra Modi's public outreach, arguing that young people could see through political messaging.

"If you want to win over the Gen Z, then making videos with different camera angles will not help. The prime minister needs to change the angle of his heart, not the angle of cameras," she said.

She also urged the government to acknowledge the concerns raised by students over the examination controversy.

"Injustice has been done with youths under your government, accept the truth. Prime Minister Narendra Modi must take responsibility," Priyanka said.
